items.title: Manga Page Parser: Comprehensive Visual Parsing through Local Story Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.34006v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding manga requires connecting who appears and who speaks with the events, character states, and relationships that unfold across panels. We study manga visual parsing through local story understanding: analyzing each double-page spread independently to capture and organize its story information in a reusable structured representation. We propose MangaParser, an agentic reading framework that jointly performs character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding within a shared multimodal conversation, without additional training or fine-tuning. The agent uses structured story memory to guide character and speaker identification, inspecting relevant image regions when uncertain and refining its predictions and story records together as evidence accumulates. Quantitative evaluations show that our parser substantially outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones. Parsing examples illustrate how a unified representation links the character and speaker predictions with narrative content and supporting evidence. We further test reusability through story question answering using outputs generated before the questions are provided. The results confirm output reusability, offering a foundation for manga translation, content retrieval, and question answering.

This extends document understanding to a culturally significant but underexplored medium with complex reading-order and dialogue structure.

items.title: When to Respond, Where to Ground: Streaming 3D Affordance Grounding
items.content: arXiv:2611.34067v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.

items.summary: StreamAff tackles streaming 3D affordance grounding, where an agent must decide both when to respond to a language request and where to locate the relevant functional part using only RGB-D observations available so far. It is a novel problem setting with robotics relevance, but the method appears scoped to a specific task rather than a broadly reusable advance.

items.title: LiveRelight: Sub-Second Global Illumination Editing for Gaussian Interiors
items.content: arXiv:2611.34226v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.

items.title: Attacking Hard-Label Large Vision-Language Models with Model-Sensitive Adversarial Patch Designs
items.content: arXiv:2611.34467v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in handling multi-modal downstream tasks, gaining increasing popularity. However, recent studies show that LVLMs are susceptible to both intentional and inadvertent attacks. Existing attackers ideally optimize adversarial perturbations with backpropagated gradients from LVLMs, thus limiting their scalability in practical scenarios as real-world LVLM applications will not provide any LVLM's gradient or details. Motivated by this research gap and counter-practical phenomenon, we propose a novel hard-label attack method for LVLMs, named HardPatch, to generate visual adversarial patches by solely querying the model. Our method provides deeper insights into how to investigate the vulnerability of LVLMs in local visual regions and generate corresponding adversarial substitution under the practical yet challenging hard-label setting. Specifically, we first split each image into uniform patches and mask each of them to individually assess their sensitivity to the LVLM model. Then, according to the descending order of sensitive scores, we iteratively select the most vulnerable patch to initialize noise and estimate gradients with further additive random noises for optimization. In this manner, multiple patches are perturbed until the altered image satisfies the adversarial condition. Extensive LVLM models and datasets are evaluated to demonstrate the adversarial nature of HardPatch. Our empirical observations suggest that with appropriate patch substitution and optimization, HardPatch can craft effective adversarial images to attack hard-label LVLMs.

The model-sensitive design provides insights into invariances and vulnerabilities of LVLMs under query-only threat models.
items.reasoning: Query-only hard-label attacks are more realistic than gradient-based attacks, making this a meaningful contribution to multimodal security. However, adversarial patch literature is well-trodden and the advance is primarily a threat-model adaptation rather than a new capability class.

items.title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
items.content: arXiv:2611.34489v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$\Omega$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.

It contributes FindEgo-1M, 1.16M ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types and 111 test settings.

items.title: Score-based Black-box Attack via Adversarial Condition Guided Diffusion Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.34564v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative models enable unrestricted adversarial attacks that aim to fool classifiers while preserving the natural appearance and semantics of the original image. However, existing diffusion-based black-box attacks largely rely on transferability from surrogates, making their effectiveness sensitive to differences between surrogate and victim. Improving transferability can also distort semantic content and degrade image quality. Moreover, retaining the original prompt to preserve fidelity leaves the diffusion model's conditional prior underused for adversarial guidance. We address these limitations by adapting score-based black-box attacks to reverse diffusion, using the victim's output probabilities to guide latent updates without accessing its gradients. We further introduce adaptive-target guidance, which uses the victim's current runner-up class as an adversarial condition to steer denoising towards the decision boundary. Because such guidance can introduce unwanted semantic changes, we also propose target-search guidance, which searches for a small perturbation of the original condition embedding using a score-based attack. This achieves comparable attack effectiveness with better image quality than runner-up guidance. Experiments on the ImageNet-Compatible dataset show that our framework outperforms transfer-based baselines in both attack effectiveness and image quality.

This avoids the quality degradation and surrogate-sensitivity issues of prior diffusion-based attacks while preserving the natural appearance and semantics of the image.
items.reasoning: Technically interesting advance in adversarial ML that removes reliance on surrogate transferability, but it is an incremental attack method in a crowded subfield; relevance is mainly to adversarial robustness evaluation rather than broad impact.

This avoids the quality degradation and surrogate-sensitivity issues of prior diffusion-based attacks while preserving the natural appearance and semantics of the image.
items.content_html: arXiv:2611.34564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models enable unrestricted adversarial attacks that aim to fool classifiers while preserving the natural appearance and semantics of the original image. However, existing diffusion-based black-box attacks largely rely on transferability from surrogates, making their effectiveness sensitive to differences between surrogate and victim. Improving transferability can also distort semantic content and degrade image quality. Moreover, retaining the original prompt to preserve fidelity leaves the diffusion model's conditional prior underused for adversarial guidance. We address these limitations by adapting score-based black-box attacks to reverse diffusion, using the victim's output probabilities to guide latent updates without accessing its gradients. We further introduce adaptive-target guidance, which uses the victim's current runner-up class as an adversarial condition to steer denoising towards the decision boundary. Because such guidance can introduce unwanted semantic changes, we also propose target-search guidance, which searches for a small perturbation of the original condition embedding using a score-based attack. This achieves comparable attack effectiveness with better image quality than runner-up guidance. Experiments on the ImageNet-Compatible dataset show that our framework outperforms transfer-based baselines in both attack effectiveness and image quality.

items.title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.33309v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.

A focused refinement of the state of the art in neural decoding rather than a paradigm shift.

items.title: SpiderSkel: Sub-Pixel Multi-Tangent 2D Skeletonization from Inscribed-Disc Geometry
items.content: arXiv:2611.33805v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Skeletonization reduces a binary shape to a compact medial representation, but pixel-grid discretization perturbs the boundary-contact geometry underlying the medial axis, creating tension among connectivity, reconstruction fidelity, and skeleton compactness. SpiderSkel is a family of training-free two-dimensional skeletonization methods built on multi-tangent inscribed-disc geometry. A tie-aware exact Euclidean distance transform retains tied nearest boundary sites rather than collapsing them to a single label; medial candidates are localised to sub-pixel positions from the inscribed disc's tangent contacts, filtered by the angular span of those contacts, and completed by connectivity-aware refinement. Across nineteen public benchmarks comprising 11,323 images of shapes, retinal vessels, cracks and roads, and document images, a single operating point fixed across datasets yields skeletons that, on every image, have exact skeleton topology under the component/hole certificate, remain fully connected, and have exact per-object reconstruction topology. The three SpiderSkel variants are the only evaluated methods to satisfy all three properties across every category; within each category, every variant is Pareto-optimal with respect to all twenty-two baselines in strict sub-pixel reconstruction Dice versus reduction rate. Incremental engines for all three variants reproduce the skeleton of a complete recomputation exactly across 23,040 verified edit steps, with median update latencies of 15.4-18.1 ms per foreground edit and 4.3-4.4 ms per canvas edit, and speedups reaching 33.0-fold on canvas edits.

items.summary: Introduces a family of training-free 2D skeletonization methods built on multi-tangent inscribed-disc geometry, retaining tied nearest boundary sites in an exact Euclidean distance transform and localizing medial candidates to sub-pixel positions. Connectivity-aware refinement balances skeleton compactness, connectivity, and reconstruction fidelity. Evaluated across nineteen public benchmarks, improving on pixel-grid-limited classical methods.
items.reasoning: Technically careful classical-geometry contribution with sub-pixel precision and a training-free design that is broadly usable; thorough benchmark coverage. Skeletonization is a mature niche area, so impact is real but bounded.

items.title: Compact Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environmentsvia On-Policy Training and Route-Bearing Output
items.content: arXiv:2611.34561v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora. Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies. Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce. In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view. We present \textbf{\paper}, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations. \paper adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass. The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion. This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits. On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights. On the \valunseen split, \paper achieves \rFinSR\% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (\rtor), averaged over three seeds, and \rRxFinSR\% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (\rxr). Inference requires \rDecMs\,ms and \rInferGB\,GiB of memory, while training takes \rCostTrainTyp\ GPU-hours on one 12\,GB consumer GPU.
items.author: Reshad Ul Karim, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md. Khalilur Rhaman, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
items.summary: This paper presents a 2-billion-parameter monocular RGB policy for vision-language navigation in continuous environments, trained with on-policy methods so that training distribution matches the states the running policy actually visits. It also introduces a route-bearing output representation that removes the dependency on image-plane waypoints being visible in the camera view. The goal is to approach the accuracy of larger 4-8B language-model-based navigation policies while remaining cheap to train and deploy on a single GPU.
items.reasoning: Addresses a practical and increasingly important problem: efficient embodied navigation without relying on large pretrained LLMs. The on-policy training insight (covering only expert-visited states with imitation labels) is a well-motivated contribution, and a 2B-parameter competitive policy would matter for real robot deployment. However, it is an incremental academic effort from a less-established group, and the abstract does not indicate SOTA claims against the strongest baselines.

items.title: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2611.33560v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs from execution feedback and retaining experience for later tasks. This process can fail when an agent treats an unsuccessful program as evidence that the task is physically impossible, ending exploration with revision budget remaining. We study this failure in Qwen3.8-27B and examine two decisions that shape skill discovery: I) how execution failures are diagnosed, and II) which lessons enter the shared skill library. Failure diagnosis requires the agent to reconstruct physical action effects from multimodal traces, while independent reproduction of a proposed repair does not require adequate task performance from its source program. We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action outcomes to guide repair and measured task success to govern skill admission. A grounded event log reports action effects and object end states from depth images and proprioception, separating sensor observations from inferred diagnoses. Verified promotion adds a development-success requirement on the source program to the existing independent reproduction check. Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign. On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points, with frozen model weights and the same program-revision budget.
items.author: Wenfang Sun, Jianghao Deng, Wenzhe Yin, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek

Studied on the existing Qwen3.8-27B model, the protocol improves two decisions: how execution failures are diagnosed from multimodal traces, and which lessons enter a shared skill library, without requiring the source program to have performed well. This makes skill discovery more robust and budget-efficient.

The contribution is a targeted protocol fix around an existing LLM rather than a new capability, so the score is moderate.

items.title: CoTAMP: Cooperative Task and Motion Planning for Quadruped Robots with Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.33911v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Some environments cannot be traversed by a single quadruped robot, for example a ledge that one robot can climb only from its partner's back or a gap that must be bridged with boxes. Solving them requires cooperative task and motion planning (TAMP). Previous works are limited to the motions of a single robot or only select actions from a predefined set of skills. We propose a framework with two parts: task planning that invents motions not defined in advance, and motion generation that realizes the invented motions. Both parts consist of large language model (LLM)-based modules and code-based modules. Task planning divides the trajectory of the whole task into steps and fixes the robot poses at the step boundaries. Motion generation produces keyframes that describe the motion of each step and turns them into a continuous trajectory through kinematic synthesis. The code-based modules check every plan and motion and return failures to the LLM-based modules for correction. The whole trajectory is then refined by trajectory optimization to satisfy the dynamics. On three simulated courses with two RAIBO2 robot models, our framework produced kinematically valid references in all 30 trials, all of which converged in trajectory optimization. Compared with several baselines, our framework showed advantages in success rate, dynamic feasibility, execution time, and generation time and cost. Project page: https://woojin8098.github.io/CoTAMP/
items.author: Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
items.summary: CoTAMP addresses cooperative task and motion planning for multiple quadruped robots in environments a single robot cannot traverse, such as ledges requiring a partner's back. The framework combines LLM-based and code-based modules to both invent novel motions not in a predefined skill set and generate the trajectories that realize them.
items.reasoning: The combination of LLM-driven task planning that can invent new motions with code-based motion generation for multi-robot cooperation is a meaningful advance over single-robot or fixed-skill TAMP work. Evaluation on challenging cooperative scenarios strengthens the contribution, though LLM planners can be brittle and hardware validation scope is unclear.

items.title: DataForgeVLA: Fully Synthetic Manipulation Demonstrations for Vision-Language-Action Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.34287v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present a dataset of 340 fully synthetic manipulation demonstrations generated from real seed data for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. The corpus contains 32,340 frames with synchronized RGB and actions across eight object categories, represented as LeRobot v2.1 episodes with H.264 video, per-frame robot states and pose-valued action labels, language task annotations, summary statistics and quality decisions. Each synthetic demonstration is produced without additional teleoperation: a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model generates a manipulation video, and RoboHaMeR recovers the corresponding robot trajectory from RGB. Quality screening accepted 300 of 340 episodes for policy fine-tuning. As preliminary evidence of feasibility, a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 accepted episodes reaches 16/20 (80%) real-world pick-and-place success on the Oreo-package task. A policy fine-tuned on 105 real teleoperated episodes achieved 18/20 (90%) under the same protocol. These results are based on one object and 20 trials per policy and are therefore reported as preliminary evidence rather than a general performance claim.
items.author: Sergei Kurchev, Iaroslav Kolomiets, Filipp Maksimov, Elizaveta Semenyakina, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Artem Lykov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou

Preliminary experiments show fine-tuning a pretrained policy on the synthetic data is feasible.

However, the scale (roughly 300 accepted episodes and 32k frames) is small and evidence of policy benefit is only preliminary, so impact depends on future scaling.

items.title: Riding the Wave: Sim-to-Real Humanoid Control on Elastic Terrain
items.content: arXiv:2611.34569v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid robots on deformable elastic terrains face a surface whose position and motion are coupled in space and time: deflection and rebound persist between contacts, and load at one foothold alters the support at others, so training must capture how each contact changes the support that follows. We present RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on such terrains. RIPPLE integrates ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh that models spatially coupled deflection, energy storage, and rebound, together with deformable contact into MJLab for GPU-parallel policy learning. Staged training then transfers rigid-ground skills to balance and jumping on these terrains using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Deployed zero-shot, the policies enable a MagicBot Z1 humanoid to balance, jump consecutively, and enter a trampoline from a rigid platform. In simulation, ElasticMembrane training holds standing success of at least 98.7% (mean over three seeds) on ElasticMembrane, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate under 0.3 m/s perturbations, whereas rigid-ground or contact-compliance training transfers poorly to the first two. A fixed policy tolerates stiffness from 0.35 to 2.8 times the training value, beds up to 7 m wide, and seven further simulated support scenarios, so transfer needs no calibration to the trampoline's stiffness. We plan to release the code soon. The interactive browser demo, videos, and scene configurations are available on the project page: https://fly-pigTH.github.io/wave_rider/

The paper addresses a genuinely hard contact-dynamics regime where terrain deflection couples across footholds. It demonstrates the frontier of humanoid locomotion beyond rigid ground.

items.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
items.content:
I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform, which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.)

I compare 2 classes of policies:

- AI R&D compute cap: A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com.
- Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago). [1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze.

Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.

I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.

Factor

Cap vs. lag/freeze

Reasoning

Capability curve shape

Compute cap (weak)

Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.

Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:

Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.

We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]

- No China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3x
- No China, uncertainty over PONR [4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x

- Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

- Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference). Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.
- Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research. Attack 7 in our previous work.

Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:

- Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training. Attack 8 in our previous work.

In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).

- Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.
- Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.
- Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).

#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.

items.title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
items.content: arXiv:2611.33639v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.
items.author: Zax Shen, Hanling Zhang, Zixu Wang
items.summary: This preregistered study evaluates how reasoning-effort settings affect AI code reviewers catching plausible-but-wrong patches, using 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified with strengthened tests, where 55 patches were wrong. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 — all existing models several weeks past release — reviewed each patch at low, medium, and high effort. High effort consistently reduced false acceptance of wrong patches (e.g., Opus 0.45 versus 0.67), a supported difference across all models.
items.reasoning: A rigorous, preregistered empirical study on an operationally important question (effort-cost trade-offs in AI code review) with clean methodology. Grounded in established Claude 5.5 models rather than new releases; generalizability is limited by scope (Django patches, SWE-bench).

items.title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.33764v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.

The work targets UN sustainability goals on energy and climate.

items.title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.33821v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.
items.author: Tong Miao, Shupeng Cheng, Xiwen Chen, Ruishan Liu
items.summary: RadOncGym is an agent-based framework where an LLM agent iteratively tunes 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking radiotherapy optimization, using a surrogate verifier for fast feedback within a fixed budget of full planning solves. Clinical relevance is high since downstream optimization is required before predicted doses become usable plans.

It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.

items.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
items.content: arXiv:2611.34400v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

items.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
items.content: arXiv:2611.34635v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.
items.author: Nikita Sorokin, Zoya Volovikova, Alexey Skrynnik, Aleksandr Panov
items.summary: ZeroHero trains small language agents (under 50 million parameters) from scratch for interactive tasks: an LLM expert provides successful trajectories for behavior-cloning pretraining, followed by PPO post-training with reasoning alignment that supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the agent's generated language. The central question is how little model capacity a specialized language agent needs. This probes the efficiency frontier for deployable agents and is relevant to edge deployment.

items.title: How Many Samples Is RL Worth? Best-of-N versus RL Post-Training for Text-to-Image Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.33232v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) on a reward that can be checked automatically has become a common last step in the training of text-to-image models. A simpler way to get more correct images is best-of-N: draw N images from the base model and keep the one that a picker prefers. We ask how many base model samples one RL sample is worth, and call this number the exchange rate. We measure it for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and its public Flow-GRPO checkpoint on 398 new prompts in the style of GenEval, the benchmark behind the RL reward, with human labels on every prompt and two automatic judges other than the reward. The answer depends on the prompt. Four fifths of the prompts do not ask for a position (for example, one object left of another). On these, the base model catches up: best-of-16 with an off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) as the picker is about as good as one RL image. A person who looks through up to 3 base images finds a correct one as often as one RL image is correct. On the prompts that ask for a position, RL is far ahead: a person finds a correct image among 8 base images for only 52% of the prompts, against 92% for one RL image. Over all prompts, our primary test, which we fixed in advance, finds best-of-16 with the VLM picker 9.3 points behind one RL image when both automatic judges must pass an image. People see a smaller gap, 5.5 and 6.5 points in two checks. FLUX.1-dev shows a similar gap in the same test. RL also solves 20 prompts that the base model misses in 128 tries, and 1,024 tries recover half of them. The automatic judges are wrong in opposite directions: a detector-based judge like the reward, as used in our primary test, reports a larger gap than people see, and VLM judges report little or none. Comparisons of RL with best-of-N should therefore check the selected images by hand.

Results vary sharply by prompt type, particularly spatial-relationship prompts versus others.

items.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
items.content: arXiv:2611.33636v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.

The result reduces computational cost and memory traffic at high-resolution stages.

items.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
items.content: arXiv:2611.33937v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.

items.summary: InstructTTS-OPD tackles instability when post-training instruction-following TTS with a single scalar reward over competing objectives (instruction adherence, pronunciation, naturalness), a common seesaw problem with GRPO. It applies on-policy distillation to better balance multi-objective optimization in TTS.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real and common failure mode in RL post-training of generative audio models and applies on-policy distillation in a fresh setting; solid applied contribution, though incremental relative to existing distillation work.

items.title: Whose Side Are You On? A Framework and Benchmark for Assessing LLM Political Stances through Politicians Social Media Posts
items.content: arXiv:2611.34098v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.

items.title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.34758v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.

The strongest method, decoded weight differences through the base model's J++-lens, ranks the backdoor-triggering token highly. A concrete interpretability tool for supply-chain safety in fine-tuning.

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.34852v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
items.author: Han Huang, Yuchen Yan, Xingyu Wu, Yijun Li, Chao Deng, Jie Liu, Jin Ma, Yongliang Shen
items.summary: DRBench Pro is a benchmark that evaluates deep research agents on structured knowledge coverage, building local knowledge trees from Wikipedia to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics tied to relations in the tree. This enables assessment of which research directions a report covers and how deeply, rather than just aggregate report quality.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated benchmark addressing a real gap in evaluating research agents on knowledge coverage and depth; the automated rubric construction is clever, though Wikipedia-derived trees may limit domain diversity.

Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

items.title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.33351v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.
items.author: Ryoichi Takase, Xian Yeow Lee, Hikaru Tomonari, Masaya Tsunokake
items.summary: Analyzes failure modes of LLM-based generation of optimization models from natural language by decomposing the task into mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing targeted datasets for each component. The study finds these components associate with distinct failure types, providing a diagnostic structure for improving reliability of end-to-end optimization modeling.
items.reasoning: A useful error-taxonomy contribution to an active area of LLM agent evaluation, with a clean decomposition methodology that others can reuse. The analysis is more diagnostic than prescriptive, and the authors appear to be from an industrial lab without top-tier visibility, keeping the score moderate.

items.title: DiffER$^2$: Diffusion Ensembles for Retrosynthesis Prediction with SMILES Adapted Particle Guidance
items.content: arXiv:2611.33557v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Computational retrosynthesis prediction has the potential to reduce development time for newly discovered drugs by automatically generating potential reactions for a target product. Data-driven approaches commonly treat this as a sequence-to-sequence generation task on SMILES strings. In this work, we construct ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for molecular generation and incorporate guidance mechanisms for improved output diversity. We propose an adaptation of particle guidance to SMILES sequence generation which significantly improves the number of unique molecules generated by diffusion ensembles while increasing top-k accuracy. These results further expand the efficacy of discrete diffusion for SMILES generation, and our empirical analyses offer new insights into the capabilities of diffusion models for chemical retrosynthesis.

items.summary: Builds ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for molecular generation toward retrosynthesis prediction, adapting particle guidance to SMILES sequence generation to improve output diversity and top-k accuracy. The work shows the adaptation significantly increases the number of unique molecules generated by diffusion ensembles, extending the efficacy of discrete diffusion for chemistry generation.
items.reasoning: A solid contribution to generative models for chemistry with a technical novelty (particle guidance adapted to SMILES) and measurable accuracy/diversity gains. Impact is within the computational chemistry and molecular ML subfield; ensembling diffusion models is compute-heavy but well-executed.

items.title: SMOTE 25 Years of Magic: What Has Been Done, What the Evidence Shows, and Whom It Reached
items.content: arXiv:2611.34511v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Background. SMOTE was published in this journal in 2002 and reviewed here at its fifteenth anniversary in 2018. At twenty-five it is cited by more than 34,000 indexed works, half of them outside computer science. Objectives. To establish what the methods built on SMOTE change, how strong the evidence for them is, and whom the technique has reached. Methods. We audited a curated corpus of 76 papers, 37 of which propose a SMOTE-family generator, and tested its coverage with a systematic search of 22,426 records in the PRISMA 2020 format. From the corpus we collected 1,756 dataset entries, 1,511 published comparisons with SMOTE and the evaluation design of 71 studies; from the search we drew 300 applications of SMOTE at random. We used an agentic AI approach to extract, screen and code under our written rules, and we report how each step was checked. Results. Every variant re-decides some of the six decisions of the SMOTE rule, and 24 of the 37 are only ever run on two classes. In their own papers, proposed methods beat SMOTE in 79.0% of the decided comparisons, but independent studies find that the gains shrink with strong learners and tuned thresholds, and that resampling damages calibration. The corpus holds 52 of the 3,097 records that pass the screen and covers the early years closely, the recent ones thinly. The reach is very wide, but a benefit at the level of outcomes is undemonstrated, four harms are documented, and an estimated 37% of applications resample the whole data set before splitting it. Conclusions. For tabular classification, a new SMOTE variant should no longer count as a contribution in itself: a new generator should be tested one decision at a time against class weighting and a tuned threshold with a strong learner, with calibration reported. We close with a selection guide, a reporting checklist of fifteen items and a research agenda.
items.author: Thanapong Intharah, Pharamut Makjaroen, Kanvara Thawarorit, Supawit Chaingam
items.summary: A 25-year audit of SMOTE and its derivatives examining what family methods actually change, the strength of supporting evidence, and adoption reach, based on a curated corpus of 76 papers, 1,756 dataset entries, 1,511 comparisons, and a PRISMA-style search of 22,426 records. Half of SMOTE's 34,000-plus citations are outside computer science, motivating the assessment of evidence quality across fields.
items.reasoning: An unusually thorough meta-research effort on one of the most cited ML techniques ever, with potential to recalibrate community beliefs about imbalanced learning. Value lies in synthesis and evidence assessment rather than new methods.

items.title: Learning to Be Truncated: Preparing LLM Checkpoints for SVD Compression
items.content: arXiv:2611.34667v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.
items.author: Chenyue Fang, Danila Mishin, Babak Falsafi
items.summary: Proposes LLift, which prepares a pretrained model's weights for SVD compression across multiple truncation ratios with a single fine-tuning step: low-rank updates learned at one ratio are merged back into the original weights, and the resulting decompositions are reused at different ranks without further fine-tuning. Demonstrated accuracy gains across ratios on LLaMA-7B.
items.reasoning: A practical efficiency contribution addressing the ratio-specific retraining burden of SVD compression; the merge-and-reuse trick is elegant. Impact is somewhat bounded by the demonstrated model scale (7B) and competition from stronger compression baselines like quantization.

items.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.34492v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

items.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
items.content: arXiv:2611.33174v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem
items.author: Junhong Huang, Xin Tong, Jun Xia
items.summary: MGMem replaces generative LLM-based indexing in long-horizon agent memory with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline that organizes recurring mentions into an incidence graph without any generative indexing calls. This addresses three problems of LLM-indexed memory: cost, non-determinism, and loss of provenance to original turns. The design promises reproducible and auditable memory across thousands of conversation turns.
items.reasoning: Addresses real pain points in the fast-growing agent memory space with a determinism-and-provenance angle that most systems ignore. The abstract suggests a solid engineering contribution, though benchmark evidence against strong generative baselines is not yet visible from the excerpt.

items.title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.34690v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

items.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.34420v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

It uses anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates over local page triplets. This targets a real structural weakness in current document VLMs with minimal architectural cost.
items.reasoning: Identifies a genuine and commonly overlooked limitation of page-independent encoding in document VLMs and offers a clean, plug-in solution. Practical and well-motivated, though incremental relative to broader architectural advances.

items.title: ArtTet: Watertight Part Meshes of Articulated Objects from Rigid-Body Rules and Partitioned Marching Tetrahedra
items.content: arXiv:2611.33382v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present ArtTet, a method that reconstructs an articulated object from multi-view observations of two articulation states and outputs one watertight mesh per rigid part together with the joints that move them. Mesh splatting gives explicit triangles, but it treats the object as one scene. It extracts a single global surface and cannot keep the triangles of different parts apart; the mesh it exports is layered, self-intersecting, and full of holes. ArtTet follows a divide-and-conquer strategy instead. We first divide the object into rigid parts with dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody registration of the two states recovers the parts and their screw joints. Rigid-body rules on attachment, contact, and swept motion then correct joint types and part labels without any part annotation. We then divide space into part cells with an articulated tetrahedral partition, and conquer each cell with its own differentiable signed distance field on a shared tetrahedral grid. In these partitioned marching tetrahedra the fields are mutually exclusive by construction, so the extracted part meshes are closed and never overlap. All part meshes are optimized jointly from the images of both states through the recovered joints. On Articulate-100, ArtTet gives the most accurate axis directions, part motions, and part geometry over all objects among methods that use no part masks, and its part meshes have virtually no open boundary edges. We also show reconstructions of real captures from the SplArt dataset.
items.author: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
items.summary: ArtTet reconstructs articulated objects from multi-view observations of two articulation states, outputting one watertight mesh per rigid part plus their screw joints. It uses divide-and-conquer with articulation and ownership inference, multibody registration, and rigid-body rules on attachments with partitioned marching tetrahedra. This solves the layered, self-intersecting, hole-ridden meshes that monolithic mesh splatting produces for articulated objects.
items.reasoning: Well-engineered pipeline producing genuinely usable part-level meshes and joint parameters, which matters for downstream graphics and robotics. Technical depth is clear, but the input requirement of two articulation states with multi-view coverage limits applicability.

items.title: CariesBench: A Hierarchical Multi-view Benchmark for Dental Caries Screening and Diagnostic Reasoning from 3D Intraoral Scans
items.content: arXiv:2611.33643v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dental caries assessment is a structured clinical process requiring lesion localization, identification of the affected tooth and surface, and severity grading rather than simple image-level recognition. 3D intraoral scans (IOS) preserve detailed dental geometry and surface morphology and support standardized rendering from complementary viewpoints, enabling fine-grained visual assessment while introducing a distinct need for anatomically grounded multi-view reasoning. Despite recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and dental vision-language benchmarks, existing evaluations do not jointly assess hierarchical arch-to-tooth-to-surface reasoning, cross-view evidence integration, and surface-level caries assessment. To address this gap, we introduce CariesBench, a hierarchical benchmark constructed from 5,932 3D IOS, comprising 85,455 standardized multi-view renderings and 133,994 clinically grounded visual question answering instances with expert quality control. CariesBench comprises three complementary task families: Arch-level Clinical Screening (ACS), Tooth-level Diagnostic Reasoning (TDR), and Structured Clinical Decision-Making (SCD). Using the CariesBench training set, we further fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct to obtain IntraoralGPT. Extensive evaluation of 24 representative baseline MLLMs reveals a substantial benchmark-level performance disparity between arch-level screening and tooth-level diagnostic reasoning, with higher accuracy on ACS than on TDR. CariesBench-specific supervision substantially improves the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, increasing the 19-task macro-average clinical accuracy from 52.7% to 69.5% and TDR Overall from 34.4% to 44.7%.

items.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology via Topology-Informed Graph Attention and Gene-Semantics Conditioning
items.content: arXiv:2611.33792v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) profiles gene expression with spatial context but remains costly, motivating models that infer expression from H&E images. Existing approaches face three key limitations: (i) a single patch embedding is often insufficient: morphologically similar regions can exhibit distinct expression due to spatial context, while naive neighborhood aggregation can over-smooth boundaries; (ii) conventional fixed, gene-indexed output heads treat genes independently and cannot directly support strict zero-shot prediction for unseen genes; and (iii) common metrics under-measure spatial pattern fidelity and boundary resolution. To address these challenges, we propose TIGEM, a topology-informed, gene-conditioned framework for histology-to-ST inference. TIGEM learns topology-aware spot representations by regularizing graph attention with tissue-level topology and morphology cues to avoid cross-compartment smoothing, and uses gene semantic modulation to replace gene-indexed heads, enabling zero-shot prediction for unseen genes. We also introduce Graph Spectral Correlation (GSC) to evaluate spatial pattern fidelity and boundary resolution complement to PCC/MSE. Across three large-scale ST datasets, TIGEM achieves overall state-of-the-art performance and significantly improved boundary prediction resolution, and further demonstrates the ability to predict expression patterns for genes unseen during training, extending prior zero-shot histology-to-ST efforts with topology-aware spatial propagation and PLM-based gene conditioning.

It also addresses over-smoothed boundaries and inadequate spatial fidelity metrics. This could reduce the cost of spatial transcriptomics experiments significantly.

However, histology-to-expression prediction is an active and competitive area, and practical validation in real genomics workflows determines ultimate impact.
