items.title: The Reference Matters: Displacement Probing for Weight-Space Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.33998v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Weight-space learning predicts a model's attributes directly from its parameters, and probing-based methods do so efficiently by reading a model's responses to learned probes. Prior work shows that probing succeeds within a Model Tree -- models fine-tuned from a shared pretrained origin -- but not why. We trace this to the shared origin itself: since a tree's leaves start from the same weights, what distinguishes them is their displacement from that origin. This motivates probing the displacement rather than the raw weight, an intervention we call the DiSplacement Probe (DSProbe). We develop this idea along two axes: extending it to second-order Gram responses, whose displacement, to first order, tracks the feature changes induced by fine-tuning; and treating the reference as a design choice, learning a shared component to subtract beyond the pretrained origin. Across four architectures on the Model Jungle benchmark, the resulting Refined-DSProbe (R-DSProbe) sets a new state of the art, matches prior accuracy with substantially fewer probes, and supports a single encoder shared across Model Trees, reducing metanetwork parameters by 3.61 times. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/DSProbe.
items.author: Haechan Shin, Hoonki Lee, Jungwoon Kang, Wooyeol Baek, Sangyeob Kim, Jongyoo Kim
items.summary: This work studies weight-space learning, where model attributes are predicted directly from parameters, and explains why probing-based methods succeed within a Model Tree of fine-tuned checkpoints. The authors attribute this to the shared pretrained origin and introduce the DiSplacement Probe (DSProbe), which probes each model's displacement from the shared base weights rather than raw weights, extending the approach to second-order Gram responses. This provides both a theoretical explanation and a practical improvement for analyzing model lineages from their parameters.

The topic is relatively niche compared to mainstream capability research, and immediate practical impact is likely limited to model analysis and forensics communities. The multi-author team and principled framing support moderate credibility, but no headline SOTA results are claimed.

items.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
items.content: arXiv:2611.34166v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $\pi_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $\mu_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

items.title: RAWPrism: A Three-Task Dataset and a Unified Model for RAW-Domain Image Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.34359v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Research on multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) has largely focused on rendered RGB images, while unified fusion across these tasks in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP) remains relatively underexplored. To support research in this setting, we introduce the RAWPrism dataset, covering all three tasks, and the RAWPrism model, a lightweight unified multi-task fusion network. The RAWPrism dataset comprises 422 usable MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from our RAW captures, together with 1,500 FMB-derived IVIF samples, in which the visible RAW inputs are reconstructed by ReRAW and their RGB counterparts rendered by CycleISP. Scene-level partitions and task-specific rendering and scoring protocols connect these resources to method development and evaluation. To our knowledge, the RAWPrism model is the first to unify MEF, MFF, and IVIF directly in the RAW domain. It combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone to support all three tasks with one 3.58M-parameter checkpoint. Together, the dataset and model support the study of shared fusion mechanisms across exposure, focus, and spectral complementarity.

items.title: Robust Recourse under Causal Graph Ambiguity
items.content: arXiv:2611.34723v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Causal algorithmic recourse recommends actions to reverse unfavorable decisions by modeling how interventions change an individual's features. Existing methods typically assume one causal graph that describes the system and account for uncertainty in the causal mechanisms. However, there usually exist several graphs that fit the same data but can predict different effects for the same action. Certain actions may achieve recourse across multiple graphs, but as the set of potential graphs grows, a single best action may become infeasible.   We propose Worst-Case Recourse and Graph-Weighted Recourse to find a low-cost action that succeeds across all candidate graphs or a specified fraction of graph weight, respectively. Assuming a set of plausible graphs, for each graph we fit Gaussian process structural equations and assess success using the posterior mean--standard-deviation criterion. We use gradient-based search to determine minimal cost actions and check the validity of the actions on fresh posterior samples. In synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, relaxing robustness, the requirement that an action succeed under every candidate graph, can increase the number of valid recommendations for recourse and lower costs of actions for both methods. In the 20-node GP benchmark, relaxation increases the number of factual instances offered recourse (coverage) from 341 to 436 out of 1,000, while the number of true successes, actions that flip the decision under the generating model, falls from 251 to 184, illustrating the coverage--validity trade-off. Accounting for graph ambiguity can help decision-makers recommend actions that remain effective even when the causal mechanisms of the system are not fully known.

items.title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
items.content: arXiv:2611.33489v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.

items.title: LatENSO v1.0: a learned latent state of the tropical Pacific for seasonal ENSO operators and forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2611.34296v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Here we present LatENSO v1.0, a machine-learning forecast system for the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) built around a learned, 32-dimensional state of the tropical Pacific. A Swin-transformer autoencoder compresses thirteen monthly-averaged ocean and atmosphere fields into 32 numbers, trained to reconstruct the fields, with no forecast target. The 32 numbers rebuild the fields as well as O(100) empirical orthogonal functions. Two seasonal operators use this state. The first is the extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO) with two directions of the learned state among its variables; we call it XRO-lat. The second is a Floquet modal operator (FMO) of three damped oscillators, which forecasts a correction added to a least-squares base forecast made from four observed predictors. We evaluate both against the recharge oscillator, XRO and a deep echo-state network (DESN), all refitted on identical data, cross-validation folds and verification windows (1981-2024). Over lead times of 1-18 months, XRO-lat reaches an anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) of 0.673, the highest of all tropical-Pacific-only (in-domain) systems and statistically indistinguishable from XRO and DESN with their eight remote-basin indices (0.685 and 0.667). From lead 15 to lead 24 it is the most skillful of all systems. Over leads 1-18, the FMO forecast (0.619) is statistically indistinguishable from every in-domain reference model (0.631-0.654). What the FMO adds to its base forecast, 0.054 in ACC, is carried by its Floquet propagation, whose generator consistently holds a prominent quasi-biennial oscillator. At leads 3-9 the FMO trails XRO, DESN and the in-domain XRO, a deficit partly attributable to its base. LatENSO combines competitive skill with trustworthiness: a compact state whose physical content can be inspected, and fully open access to code, weights and data.

items.summary: LatENSO v1.0 compresses thirteen monthly ocean-atmosphere fields into a 32-dimensional learned latent state via a Swin-transformer autoencoder, then uses that state in two lightweight seasonal forecasting operators for El Nino-Southern Oscillation prediction. The compact state reconstructs fields as well as hundreds of empirical orthogonal functions, and the hybrid ML-plus-dynamical-operator approach yields an interpretable seasonal forecast system. This demonstrates how learned low-dimensional states can improve climate forecasting efficiency and transparency.
items.reasoning: Creative hybrid of learned representation and classical reduced-order operators with real forecasting value; domain-specific impact and small-scale evaluation keep the score moderate.

What the FMO adds to its base forecast, 0.054 in ACC, is carried by its Floquet propagation, whose generator consistently holds a prominent quasi-biennial oscillator. At leads 3-9 the FMO trails XRO, DESN and the in-domain XRO, a deficit partly attributable to its base. LatENSO combines competitive skill with trustworthiness: a compact state whose physical content can be inspected, and fully open access to code, weights and data.

items.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
items.content: arXiv:2611.34419v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

items.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34863v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv

This reduces compute for video object segmentation without retraining.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.33499v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

items.summary: The paper evaluates closed-weight LLMs, including Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning and GPT-4.1 configurations, on authentic conversational African American English drawn from the CORAAL corpus rather than the synthetic or stylized data used in prior bias work. It runs feature classification and next-turn generation tasks over 100 six-turn segments. This better reflects how models encounter AAE in real chatbot deployment and grounds sociolinguistic bias evaluation in genuine speech data.

items.title: PINN-Slicer: Exploiting Rotational Symmetry to Solve the Photon Orbit Equation Around a Black Hole
items.content: arXiv:2611.33953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically struggle with long-horizon domains, often requiring the network to be retrained as the domain grows. We present PINN-Slicer, a method for second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, $\ddot{u} = G(u, \dot{u})$, which exploits the invariance of this class of equations under translations of the independent variable. A single PINN, embedded within a solution ansatz that enforces the initial conditions explicitly, is trained on a thin slice of the independent variable using Sobol-sampled initial conditions. The PINN is then deployed recursively, slice-by-slice, across the full domain. We demonstrate PINN-Slicer on the nonlinear equation that describes photon orbits around a black hole, and reach a point-by-point root-mean-square error (RMSE) below $10^{-3}$ in $u = r_s/r$ (the inverse radial coordinate in units of the Schwarzschild radius) relative to a finite-difference reference solution. A key advantage of PINN-Slicer is that a single trained network generalizes to any orbital initial condition within the training range, without retraining. In addition, PINN-Slicer can cope with solution domains that may not be known a priori.

It is demonstrated on the nonlinear photon-orbit equation around a black hole.

items.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
items.content: arXiv:2611.34179v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.

This offers an empirically grounded framework for how AI vocabulary evolves.

items.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.31990v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
items.author: Dovud Asadov, Rustambek Urokov, Qobiljon Toshnazarov, Abduaziz Kayumov, Mardon Hazratov, Husanboy Mansuraliyev

The authors estimate this correlation across four masked diffusion LMs and show that the best marginal-only predictors are off by roughly one bit, with much of their accuracy inherited from a simple bound. The work provides useful theoretical grounding for decoder design in diffusion LMs.

items.title: StyleID++: Position-Decoupled and Structure-Coherent Style Retrieval across Diffusion Architectures
items.content: arXiv:2611.33323v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Attention injection offers a remarkably simple route to training-free style transfer: content queries retrieve style keys and values inside a pretrained diffusion model. We show that this operation also creates an overlooked failure mode. Position signals that are useful within one image become a spurious shared coordinate system across two spatially unrelated images, causing content tokens to favor style tokens at similar coordinates. This cross-image positional leakage appears in both convolutional U-Nets and diffusion transformers (DiTs), despite their different position mechanisms. Removing the positional shortcut exposes a second problem: unconstrained global retrieval lets related content tokens select incompatible style regions, producing fragmented appearance. We present StyleID++, a training-free framework that addresses the two problems jointly. Position-Decoupled Retrieval reduces coordinate-dependent matching through circular padding in U-Nets and injection-only RoPE removal in DiTs, while preserving native position modeling elsewhere. Affinity-Coherent Refinement then regularizes style assignments with the content self-attention graph, encouraging structurally related tokens to retrieve compatible style evidence. We quantify the leakage with a coordinate--centroid correlation and a permutation test on the style reference. The permutation error can be driven to zero in both backbones, which identifies the position mechanism as the carrier of the leakage, and StyleID++ obtains the best ArtFID of all methods we compare.

items.summary: StyleID++ identifies and fixes cross-image positional leakage in attention-injection style transfer, where positional signals create a spurious shared coordinate system between unrelated content and style images in both U-Nets and diffusion transformers. Removing the positional shortcut exposes incoherent global retrieval, which the paper addresses with structure-coherent retrieval. This yields more reliable training-free style transfer across diffusion architectures.

items.title: Synchronizing Cameras via 3D Object Relationships
items.content: arXiv:2611.33387v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, we synchronize multiple videos of the same dynamic event through object relationships. Driven by dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis, many recent synchronization methods rely on pixel-level evidence, such as point correspondences across views or the photometric losses of a reconstructed scene. In dynamic scenes, however, fast motion and occlusions make the moving regions that carry much of the timing information hard to match across views. We thus propose to bring back the traditional wisdom that objects are reliable cues for global reasoning about cameras. Measured in 3D, the relationships between objects, such as the distance between two people, are stable across all views up to scale; they can serve as cues for alignment. To compare these relationships across cameras, we only need the identity of each object in every view, as the cues are relational. We obtain these identities by giving a vision-language model a few frames of every camera and prompting it to identify the objects in the scene. We then segment and track each identified object through every video with an open-vocabulary segmentor. To obtain the 3D locations of objects, we use a pretrained depth estimator. Where depth or segmentation fails, we complement these 3D cues with 2D motion from point tracks. Finally, we synchronize the cameras by finding the temporal offsets at which the cues of different cameras agree best, first for each camera pair and then for all cameras jointly with robust optimization. We evaluate our method on four standard benchmarks, outperforming the state of the art.
items.author: Sujong Shin, Sang-Il Choi, Kwang Moo Yi
items.summary: This paper synchronizes multiple videos of a dynamic event using 3D object relationships, such as inter-person distances, which are stable across views up to scale, instead of fragile pixel-level correspondences. The approach revives object-level reasoning where fast motion and occlusion defeat photometric or point-based matching. This is valuable for dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis pipelines.
items.reasoning: Simple, well-motivated insight with robustness advantages in exactly the hard regimes (fast motion, occlusion) that matter for multi-view dynamics. Incremental but technically clean contribution to multi-view geometry.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.33387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we synchronize multiple videos of the same dynamic event through object relationships. Driven by dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis, many recent synchronization methods rely on pixel-level evidence, such as point correspondences across views or the photometric losses of a reconstructed scene. In dynamic scenes, however, fast motion and occlusions make the moving regions that carry much of the timing information hard to match across views. We thus propose to bring back the traditional wisdom that objects are reliable cues for global reasoning about cameras. Measured in 3D, the relationships between objects, such as the distance between two people, are stable across all views up to scale; they can serve as cues for alignment. To compare these relationships across cameras, we only need the identity of each object in every view, as the cues are relational. We obtain these identities by giving a vision-language model a few frames of every camera and prompting it to identify the objects in the scene. We then segment and track each identified object through every video with an open-vocabulary segmentor. To obtain the 3D locations of objects, we use a pretrained depth estimator. Where depth or segmentation fails, we complement these 3D cues with 2D motion from point tracks. Finally, we synchronize the cameras by finding the temporal offsets at which the cues of different cameras agree best, first for each camera pair and then for all cameras jointly with robust optimization. We evaluate our method on four standard benchmarks, outperforming the state of the art.

items.title: DualCast: Dual-Image Conditioned Diffusion Transformers for Digital Human E-Commerce Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.33734v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.

items.title: Revisiting Monocular In-Hand Object Scanning: Dataset, Pose Estimation, and Surface Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.33824v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In-Hand Object Scanning (IHOS) from monocular video captured by a commodity smartphone holds immense potential to democratize 3D digitization for non-expert users, facilitating applications in digital archiving, augmented reality, and custom fabrication. Yet, IHOS remains largely understudied due to a lack of realistic datasets and systematic benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce ToysRUs, a high-quality dataset featuring diverse figurines captured by 4K Ultra High-Definition (UHD) monocular videos. Studying IHOS from first principles, we examine structure-from-motion (SfM) for camera pose estimation, which is key to IHOS. We identify two key challenges: small baselines between consecutive frames, and sparse feature matches across large-view, long-range frames, further exacerbated by dynamic hand occlusions. Guided by these insights, we propose performing SfM on video sub-sequences sampled at sufficient angular intervals, and iteratively stitches the corresponding sub-trajectories into a unified global trajectory. Furthermore, for high-fidelity surface reconstruction, we introduce occlusion-aware 2D Gaussian Splatting, which incorporates opacity rendering and omits the opacity loss on hand regions. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing approaches, including neural implicit representations and 3D foundation models, in both geometric accuracy and photometric fidelity.

Datasets plus systematic analysis fill a real gap in an understudied task.

items.title: Where to Approximate: Understanding and Accelerating Looped Multi-View Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.33948v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Looped multi-view reconstruction refines scene features by repeatedly applying a shared transformer block. Making these updates cheaper requires knowing how an approximation at one step affects the rest of the refinement. We study this with paired interventions in D\'ej\`a View and stacked reconstruction transformers, separating the error an approximation injects, how that error propagates, and how it affects the output. In D\'ej\`a View, approximation errors are attenuated more strongly than matched random perturbations under a scale-adjusted state-error measure, and a local Jacobian decomposition separates the contribution of channel gating from the response to spatial error structure. Spatial approximations made early benefit from subsequent refinement, whereas cross-step reuse depends on which quantity is cached and how reuse steps are spaced. At equal final norm, approximation errors change the predicted rotations 1.55 times as much as random errors. These findings guide our proposed method, which reduces spatial resolution and pools keys and values early in refinement, then interleaves attention-output reuse with full attention, and is adapted through lightweight self-distillation. Across five reconstruction benchmarks, the balanced configuration runs $1.63\times$ faster than the official 16-step D\'ej\`a View model with a 1.86-point reduction in average pose AUC@$3^\circ$. At matched latency, it exceeds the interpolated curve of a trained baseline using full refinement blocks by 4.73 points in AUC@$3^\circ$ and improves the corresponding geometry metrics.

A careful mechanistic analysis with practical speedup implications.

items.title: ScaleCurve: From Constant Scale to Consistent Motion for World-Space Human Mesh Recovery
items.content: arXiv:2611.34005v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World-space human mesh recovery can lose spatial consistency even when camera-space body estimates are accurate. A single sequence-wide scale resolves global scale ambiguity but cannot correct local scale distortion along a reconstructed camera path. We present ScaleCurve, a framework that estimates time-varying metric corrections from human-ground geometry. We construct scale observations by comparing predicted foot geometry with locally fitted ground planes. Joint temporal optimization downweights inconsistent observations and couples neighboring scale estimates, allowing calibration to adapt along the camera path without freely following measurement noise. We scale camera translation increments and integrate them into a calibrated trajectory. With this camera fixed, we refine the lifted body motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics, while restricting global trajectory rescaling. ScaleCurve achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics on both EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D. Consistent gains across three HMR backbones demonstrate its compatibility with diverse body estimates without retraining. Code will be made publicly available.
items.author: Sanghyeon Lee, Jong Taek Lee
items.summary: ScaleCurve addresses local scale distortion in world-space human mesh recovery, where a single sequence-wide scale factor cannot correct inconsistencies along a reconstructed camera path. It estimates time-varying metric corrections by comparing predicted foot geometry against locally fitted ground planes, then jointly optimizes temporally to downweight noisy observations and couple neighboring scale estimates. This improves spatial consistency of reconstructed human motion, important for AR/VR and motion capture applications.
items.reasoning: A sensible, targeted geometric refinement with a principled temporal optimization formulation. The contribution is incremental within human mesh recovery rather than opening a new capability, and evaluation details are truncated, but the foot-ground calibration idea is practical and well grounded.

items.title: TaCo: Rethinking Correlation for Visual Tracking on Edge Devices
items.content: arXiv:2611.34084v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lightweight trackers have replaced cross-correlation with attention, and on low-power edge hardware they pay for it, since memory-bound softmax, normalization and reshaping operators of attention cost far more time than their arithmetic suggests. Benchmarking efficient trackers on an edge Neural Processing Unit (NPU) and an Arm CPU under one numerically validated protocol, we find that correlation trackers are the fast ones, but they lag in accuracy unless they adopt a ViT backbone, which brings attention back. We revisit what correlation lacks. Template--search interaction serves two roles: conditioning the search features on the target and matching them against it spatially. Attention does both, whereas correlation only matches, and does so on features extracted without knowledge of the target. We present TaCo (Target-aligned Correlation), which supplies the missing conditioning without attention by letting the template enter the per-frame network only as operands computed once per video. A descriptor of the target scales and shifts the search features channel by channel inside the backbone, and kernels aligned with the target box, each with a weight predicted from the template, correlate with them in one matrix product. With the backbone fixed, our correlation remains essential while incurring negligible NPU overhead, offering a better speed-accuracy trade-off than the attention-based interactions we tested. TaCo-T achieves 62.3% LaSOT AUC at 184 FPS on the Rockchip RV1126B NPU and 96 FPS on a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU, 3.0x and 3.5x the NPU speed of HiT-Tiny and AsymTrack-T at higher accuracy. TaCo-B reaches 65.6% at 50 FPS on the NPU, more than twice the speed of HiT-Base, AsymTrack-B and LightFC-vit, again at higher accuracy. Code and models are available at https://github.com/TsingWei/TaCo-Tracker.
items.author: Qingmao Wei, Fagui Liu, Quan Tang
items.summary: TaCo benchmarks efficient visual trackers on edge NPUs and Arm CPUs under a validated protocol, showing that attention-based operations are memory-bound and slow on edge hardware even though they dominate recent tracker design. The paper reintroduces correlation-style interaction augmented with ViT features to recover the conditioning role that attention provides, targeting fast and accurate edge tracking.

items.title: Spe3DUp: Faithful Trajectory Distillation for Fast Image-to-3D Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34141v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent 3D generative models can produce high-quality meshes with complex structures and fine geometric details, with broad applications in games, film, and digital design. However, high-quality generation typically relies on long multi-step sampling processes that repeatedly evaluate large networks, leading to long inference times. At the same time, reference-driven tasks such as game-asset reconstruction and product digitization demand close correspondence to the input image: generated geometry must faithfully reconstruct the specific reference object. Acceleration must therefore reduce sampling computation while preserving the model's ability to reconstruct that object. To enable fast and faithful 3D generation, we introduce Spe3DUp, a coarse-to-fine framework based on Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD). FTD directly supervises few-step students with the teacher's input-conditioned denoising trajectories to preserve its generation behavior. We apply FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement, compressing both sampling processes while maintaining correspondence to the reference input. We further accelerate the complete mesh-generation pipeline with efficient geometry decoding and parallel remeshing. Experiments show that Spe3DUp maintains geometric quality and input correspondence close to those of the teacher, accelerates the coarse and refinement DiTs by 10.0x and 19.9x, respectively, and achieves a 7.7x end-to-end speedup over the original teacher pipeline.

items.summary: Spe3DUp accelerates image-to-3D generation via trajectory distillation that reduces multi-step sampling while preserving faithful reconstruction of the reference object. It targets applications like game-asset reconstruction and product digitization where close geometric correspondence to the input image is essential.
items.reasoning: Distillation-based acceleration of 3D generative models is an active and commercially relevant area; the emphasis on reference faithfulness during acceleration is a sensible angle. However, the approach is incremental within a crowded field of sampling-acceleration methods.

items.title: Semantic State Reading for Joint Image-Semantic Diffusion Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2611.34279v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pretrained visual representations improve diffusion-transformer training, yet exploiting both global context and local spatial structure requires deciding which semantic states to model and how to access them. We introduce Semantic State Reading (SSR), which jointly denoises image latents, a global CLS token encoding image-level context, and a compact patch state preserving spatial correspondence. SSR couples this global-local modeling with distinct reading paths: local states are fused with corresponding image tokens at the input, while independent projections inject the current global state into every transformer block. Both semantic scopes thus remain accessible throughout denoising. Ablations show complementary benefits from local-state modeling and repeated global reading, and semantic-trajectory interventions alter image layout under a fixed class label. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, SiT-XL/2 with SSR reaches or surpasses the reference FIDs of SiT, REPA, and Representation Entanglement for Generation (REG) with $100\times$, $40\times$, and $2\times$ fewer training iterations, respectively. SSR achieves unguided FID 1.78 at 2M iterations and FID 1.34 with classifier-free guidance alone. Combining classifier-free guidance with autoguidance yields FID 1.31 at 1M iterations, achieving the best FID in our main comparison table.

items.title: CADENCE: Sensor-GroundedWorld-Consistent Gaussian SLAM for Collaborative Mobile Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.34549v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Collaborative reconstruction with consumer phones promises faster and more complete indoor maps. However, heterogeneous devices introduce degraded observations and unreliable cross-device associations, so a single poor contributor or incorrect match can corrupt the shared Gaussian map. To address this, we propose \textbf{CADENCE}, a collaborative Gaussian simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system that separates finding cross-device matches from deciding whether and how peer observations update the map. To find matches, a sensor-grounded regional memory summarizes committed observations and ranks candidate peer regions using appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality. Deterministic geometric verification and optional physical checks then decide which of the proposed matches are accepted. Once a match is accepted, separate cue-based confidences control how its observations contribute to pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory. As a result, useful depth can still contribute even when color is unreliable. Throughout this process, local tracking remains isolated from mapping, verification, and networking. We evaluate CADENCE on eight Matterport3D houses that were not used to train the memory. On these houses, regional memory achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of $0.95$ to $0.97$ and thus outperforms appearance retrieval, while verification keeps false-link rates below $0.5\,\%$. Furthermore, soft confidence weighting reduces the mean receiver peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) loss from $2.66$ to $1.05$\,dB across eight degradations while retaining useful peer depth. Finally, using inertial and platform motion, CADENCE tracks all twelve held-out iPhone scans with a mean absolute trajectory error of $6.98$\,cm, and its refined maps achieve better average rendering quality than the baselines.
items.author: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
items.summary: CADENCE is a collaborative Gaussian SLAM system for multi-phone indoor reconstruction that decouples cross-device match finding from deciding whether peer observations should update the shared map, using sensor-grounded regional memory with appearance, relative pose, gravity, and barometric cues plus deterministic geometric verification.
items.reasoning: Collaborative phone-based reconstruction is a practical goal, and the robustness-oriented design against poor contributors and false matches is sensible. Appears to be an early-stage system from a less-established team; impact hinges on real-world validation.

items.title: Physics-Guided Generative Modelling of Oxy-Combustion Flame Images: From Conditional LSGANs to Denoising Diffusion Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.34568v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Validating industrial oxy-combustion burner designs traditionally requires costly experimental campaigns in which each operating condition is physically reproduced on an instrumented rig and imaged via OH* chemiluminescence, rendering iterative design exploration prohibitively slow. This work develops deep generative surrogate models that map a 15-dimensional vector of continuous operating parameters (thermal power, swirl numbers, momentum ratios, mixture fractions, etc.) directly to a $512\times64$ heat-release flame image, trained on 1,609 experimental samples from the OXYTEC dual-swirl non-premixed oxy-combustion database. Two complementary generative paradigms are investigated, as they offer opposite strengths for surrogate modelling: a custom spatially-anchored conditional least-squares GAN (cLSGAN-L1-CBN), whose single-pass generation enables near-instantaneous inference, and a custom physics-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM), whose iterative sampling favours the smooth, continuous heat-release gradients of fluid flows. Both are validated through ablation on a stratified held-out test set. The optimized cLSGAN reaches RMSE 0.022 and FID 20.68 and generates an image in about 20 ms on a mobile workstation GPU, though extended training leaves its texture realism unchanged; the DDPM improves steadily over long training horizons, reaching RMSE 0.019 and FID 20.29 at 40,000 epochs, at the cost of roughly thirty seconds per image on the same hardware --- three orders of magnitude slower than the adversarial surrogate. A nearest-neighbour analysis traces the persistent worst-case errors to sparsely sampled regions of the parameter space, and a parameter-sensitivity study confirms smooth, physically consistent responses to perturbed inputs. These results demonstrate that carefully guided generative models can act as reliable visual surrogates for combustion experiments.

items.title: Seeing the Right Context: Grounded On-Policy Distillation for Remote Sensing
items.content: arXiv:2611.34700v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Remote sensing scene understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret queried targets in relation to nearby objects and surrounding structures, which serve as spatial references or define the scope of an answer. However, standard answers and bounding boxes often leave these contextual relationships implicit. Thus, we construct GeoContext-5K to make them explicit in 5,394 training pairs for visual question answering (VQA), with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions. GeOPD uses these annotations for on-policy distillation, guiding a frozen teacher with region marks on the full image and a visual fact while preserving surrounding spatial references. It prioritizes teacher corrections that agree with the shift in the student's next token distribution when evidence is restored. A complementary objective weights the contrast between the student's scores on the two views by how much masking lowers the teacher's log probability for the same sampled token. Experiments on five remote sensing VQA benchmarks show that GeOPD outperforms the evaluated open-source MLLMs and matched post-training baselines, improving over the 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average. The dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/YeeCharm/GeOPD.

items.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.34877v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace

items.title: Structure-Aware Multimodal Retrieval Under Data Scarcity, Privacy Constraints and Out-of-Domain Content
items.content: arXiv:2611.33649v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.

items.title: Lab2Sim: Agentic Generation of Interactive Laboratory Equipment from Operation Videos
items.content: arXiv:2611.33705v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the appearance, structure, and joint motions of real equipment remains challenging. Existing asset generation methods struggle to directly generate simulation assets for all equipment observed in operation videos and to faithfully reproduce the appearance, joint motions, and internal cavities of the real equipment. To address the challenge, we present Lab2Sim, an agentic framework that generates editable, simulation-ready laboratory equipment assets from egocentric or multi-view operation videos. Lab2Sim comprises four specialized agents. The Evidence Agent combines video observations with laboratory knowledge to specify equipment parts, materials, and functional requirements, which guide the Asset Agent in constructing editable Blender assets. The independent Verifier checks the generated geometry and appearance against the evidence and requirements, providing targeted feedback for revision. The Simulation Integration Agent converts verified Blender assets into simulation instances with physical properties and articulated mechanisms, using execution feedback to refine their behavior. Experiments on human and robot laboratory scenes show that Lab2Sim achieves higher visual fidelity and stronger interaction capability than coding-agent and real-to-sim baselines, including a Codex baseline using the same underlying model. We further demonstrate valve-controlled drainage and use the generated asset library to reproduce laboratory scenes and operations in RoboTwin, supporting reusable simulation environments for robotic laboratory tasks.

items.title: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.33721v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.

items.title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
items.content: arXiv:2611.33731v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

items.title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
items.content: arXiv:2611.33739v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation. We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs' verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors. Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A $2\times2$ ablation study of RegHarness's two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46. These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.

It operates for the RATs agent team without a VLA policy or demonstrations. The work targets under-controlled persistence behavior in code-generating robot agents.

The framework is tightly coupled to one agent system, limiting demonstrated generality, and the contribution is harness engineering.

These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.

items.title: DynaRC: Dynamics-Robust 4-D Radar Relocalization with Rate-Adaptive Sequence Matching
items.content: arXiv:2611.34453v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Four-dimensional millimeter-wave radar measures radial velocity within a single scan and remains resilient under adverse weather and visibility. Yet sparse directional returns, moving objects and occlusion make place matching ambiguous. We propose DynaRC, a dynamics-robust framework encompassing single-frame retrieval and sequence relocalization. Doppler evidence separates static returns and masks motion-affected cells in a polar descriptor; median ring keys retrieve candidates. Its sequence variant, Seq_DynaRC, couples endpoint-anchored rate alignment and candidate-index voting with ordered verification to associate the latest scan under unequal map/query advancement, without odometry or cloud accumulation. Across four indoor and outdoor map--query pairs, Seq_DynaRC achieves the highest conditional localization success within 2m among tested methods. On a campus-road revisit under changing traffic, success reaches 91.8%, exceeding descriptor-matched SeqSLAM by 55.0 percentage points when each method retains all its published outputs; output availability is reported separately. Code and indoor/outdoor dynamic 4D radar data are available.

items.title: FeaXDrive2: Body-Scene Spatial Grounding for Feasibility-Aware Generative Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.34658v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body-scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM-Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body-scene spatial grounding.
items.author: Bo Leng, Baoyun Wang, Wenxin Wen, Ming Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Ran Yu, Chongfeng Wei, Zhuoren Li, Lu Xiong

It constructs spatial queries from vehicle-body corners, dynamically updates visual sampling during Flow steps, and applies rollout-consistent safety fine-tuning combining high-risk trajectories. This addresses a real failure mode where generative planners produce apparently feasible but body-violating trajectories.

items.title: Operationalizing a pre-training R&D pause
items.content:
OpenAI’s Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki recently said:

“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it.” [emphasis mine].

Inspired by Jakub’s request, I propose an industry standard for pacing the frontier: halt pre-training R&D for 4 months. More specifically:

- Limit on development: No stronger pre-trains, or algorithmic and data improvements that could lead to stronger pre-trains in the future if used.
- Key metric: Compute spent on pre-training R&D (defined in the appendix), verified by a third-party auditor; to enforce our development limit, we’d limit this compute spend to 0. For added assurance, we should also ensure that no lower perplexity models are trained, and generally we should ensure that there are no large-scale (10^24 FLOP or more) pre-training runs.
- What we’d need to achieve before going beyond the limit: Wait 4 months, and then decide whether pre-training R&D is now a good idea.

# Discussion

Why not just cap perplexity? Perhaps the most natural pacing proposal inspired by OpenAI’s transparency about perplexity would be: “Don’t train models with lower perplexity for the next 4 months”. While capping perplexity is a good idea, it has some limitations. Halting pre-training R&D addresses two key limitations of just capping perplexity:...
items.author: Alek Westover
items.summary: Responding to OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki's call for common development limits tied to trackable metrics, the author proposes a concrete industry standard: a four-month halt to pre-training R&D, operationalized as zero pre-training R&D compute spend verified by third-party auditors, plus checks that no lower-perplexity or large-scale (10^24+ FLOP) pre-trains occur. The post attempts to translate vague frontier-pacing rhetoric into an enforceable mechanism. It is governance proposal work rather than technical research.

items.title: AI safety grassroots work needs funding and volunteers
items.content:
This post – mostly a roundup of the AI safety grassroots organizations – was written collaboratively. Most of the individual organization summaries were written by the organizations themselves, and the claims have not been independently verified. Vael Gates, along with another anonymous author, helped assemble the information and provides some commentary, since Vael previously worked in grassroots advocacy full-time (founded Humans in Control). Views expressed here are in Vael’s personal capacity, not on behalf of their employer or any affiliated organizations.  Inclusion does not imply endorsement of every organization or organizational tactic. Many views are lightly held.

 

Vael’s overall takes:

- The window of opportunity to slow down AI is likely short, and not enough people are acting on that.
- Grassroots orgs have been very underfunded compared to other parts of the AIS ecosystem, in 501(c)(3) and also 501(c)(4).
- Underfunding orgs can cause them to develop a scarcity mindset. Scarcity mindset can lead to orgs not acting, in situation where they might otherwise ambitiously realize their impact.
- More funding would be useful in terms of weeks, not months.
- The grassroots space is not covered, and this is not common knowledge. Arguably grassroots advocacy (also comms advocacy) is the most underfunded area in AI safety given its urgency and potential.
- Grassroots work takes time, moving money takes time, and effectively converting money to impact takes time.
- In summary: We should be aggressively funding grassroots organizations as soon as possible, so that they have enough time to apply that money effectively.
- Vael would prefer that basically all the orgs below were substantially funded: $2M-$20M each. If you’re planning a large donation or want to be a supervolunteer, feel free to DM and Vael can send their top 3-5 recs shortlist, or direct you to others who have opinions.

items.title: OpenAudit: Platform for Safety Evaluations of Models, Orgs, and Methods
items.content:
# TL;DR

- OpenAudit ( openaudit.com) hosts independent safety evaluations of models, organizations, and methods. It tries to answer the question: "How prepared are we to develop and release AI safely?", while incentivizing positive hill-climbing.
- Walkthrough - We recommend the interactive Get Started Tutorial.
- Contributions - A "choose-your-own-adventure" AI safety contribution prompt guides you through an end-to-end project, from ideation to submission.
- What We Need - Advisors, collaborators, and your feedback and contributions -especially better model evaluations and safety methods.

# What is OpenAudit and why does it exist?

OpenAudit independently evaluates three main entities in AI safety: the models, the organizations, and the safety methods (both white-box and black-box). It's a platform that aims to be informative, while enabling collaboration and coordination. OpenAudit wants to incentivize positive hill-climbing by putting a verifiable rating/ranking on everything.

## Model Evaluations

OpenAudit runs evaluations on models and assigns a percentage rating for each one, judged by "Should this model be widely deployed, based on its safety evaluations and capabilities?". We heavily caveat that current model evaluations are underpowered. (See Limitations and Concerns - a high model rating does not mean a safe model.)

You can view ranked results by specific model evaluations rather than by models. Here's the AgentHarm evaluation - note again the "outdated evaluation" disclaimer.

OpenAudit records and lets you view full transcripts of evaluations. Here, Claude Haiku finds and reports LGBT-supporting accounts on Twitter in AgentHarm. OpenAudit currently shows 16,000+ flagged chats like this across 20 models.

## Organization Evaluations

Organizations on OpenAudit are primarily ranked by the strength of their safety commitments and how independently verifiable their commitments are....

items.title: Inner-Quines and Alignment
items.content:
A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. Remarkably, due to Kleene’s recursion theorem a quine exists in any Turing-complete programming language.[1]

AI abilities have skyrocketed recently with no signs of slowing down. This makes the need for ensuring their alignment urgent. The models themselves might help us with this. Right now we are in a situation analogous to the first attempts at writing a quine: the models are powerful enough to show properties of simpler or more idealized systems than themselves, as shown by their achievements in mathematics and theoretical computer science.

What would rigorous alignment look like? Something that would get us to trust an agent would be

- a mathematical model of the agent or the training process that led to it;
- a mathematical model of a set of constraints for the agent behavior;
- a proof that (with high probability) the agent respects the constraints while it is in situations.

The models’ mathematical abilities have progressed arguably even faster than their broader capabilities, which gives hope that the mathematical abilities can catch up: model generations that are able to perform the proof in (3) for a given  and  for increasingly more complex agents until that set of agents eventually includes themselves....
items.author: Valentin Hartmann
items.summary: This LessWrong post draws an analogy between quines (self-reproducing programs enabled by Kleene's recursion theorem) and AI alignment, arguing that sufficiently capable models may be able to reason about and verify properties of systems as complex as themselves or more so. The author suggests this self-reference capacity could be leveraged so that frontier models assist in their own alignment verification, much as quines circumvent the apparent barrier that programs can only output simpler programs.
items.reasoning: A creative conceptual link between recursion theory and alignment, but the visible content is largely introductory framing without formal results, experiments, or a worked-out proposal. Novel idea worth exploring, though it is speculative philosophy rather than rigorous research.

items.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

items.summary: CA-RAG conditions retrieval on ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations, targeting compliance-sensitive long-form generation where semantically relevant retrieval omits information needed for mandatory clauses. Retrieval-only evaluation with manual annotation shows consistent gains, such as Precision@6 improving from 0.5268 to 0.5692 across retrieval budgets. The work argues evidence selection should optimize for structural obligations, not just semantic relevance.
items.reasoning: A targeted, well-motivated RAG extension for a real and under-served use case (regulatory compliance documents). Gains are modest and retrieval-only evaluation does not yet show end-to-end generation benefits, but the constraint-conditioning idea is reusable.

items.title: HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants
items.content: arXiv:2611.34624v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
items.author: Yifei Xu, Li Yu, Zhaoyang Liu, Ce Wang, Sen Huang, Yanyan Shen, Yun Lin, Linpeng Huang, Hong Mei
items.summary: HoMe is an evaluation-driven framework for optimizing the harness (code, prompts, configurations) of memory systems for long-running AI assistants, iteratively generating candidates by editing any previously evaluated harness. It combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms and localize them to responsible sessions and harness components. This addresses the largely manual, ad hoc process of building agent memory harnesses.
items.reasoning: A practical automation of harness engineering for agent memory systems with a sensible failure-localization design; useful for practitioners but the contribution is engineering-oriented rather than scientifically novel.
