items.title: Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping
items.content: arXiv:2611.34019v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are important for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results showed that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type mapping when using TabPFN. However, AEF embeddings yielded comparable results, achieving accuracies of 0.91 for agricultural LULC and 0.85 for irrigation-type mapping, while reducing the need for extensive data processing and manual feature engineering typically required for satellite products. Spatial LULC mapping using TabPFN achieved comparable overall accuracies (0.85-0.86) across the three feature configurations, but revealed substantial differences in mapped tree cover, ranging from 14.57% for surface reflectance to 29.79% for AFE. Physical probing revealed that AEF embeddings strongly encode spectral indices (A30-SWIR: rho=0.58-0.67), (A38-NDMI: rho=-0.72), vegetation (A49-NDVI: rho = 0.72-0.73), and SAR structure (A25-VH: rho = 0.71). Future research should focus on enhancing the interpretability of embedding-based approaches by incorporating physical knowledge to develop more transparent and trustworthy AI systems for agricultural applications.

items.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34230v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

items.title: Calibration of Neuromusculoskeletal Models Using Differentiable Physics: Recommendations for Improving Model Accuracy
items.content: arXiv:2611.34428v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Differentiable physics has shown potential to usher in a new paradigm in human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) model calibration. Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.

items.summary: This paper systematically compares previously separately-evaluated modules for calibrating human neuromusculoskeletal models via differentiable physics, on a common differentiable upper-limb model. It provides recommendations for improving calibration accuracy while retaining the speed advantages of gradient-based optimization over traditional methods.
items.reasoning: Useful methodological consolidation for a specialized simulation domain, with practical recommendations. The comparison-study nature limits novelty, but differentiable-physics calibration is an emerging technique where systematic guidance is valuable.

items.title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
items.content: arXiv:2611.34539v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

items.summary: EPPC-CARE is an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors in patient portal messages, producing triplets of text span, communication code, and sub-code. Built on 5,516 annotations from 867 messages, it was evaluated against six open-weight LLMs and supervised fine-tuning baselines. It matters for automating labor-intensive clinical communication analysis.

items.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
items.content: arXiv:2611.34745v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.

items.title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.34811v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

items.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
items.content: arXiv:2611.34899v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.   Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

items.title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
items.content: arXiv:2611.33364v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.

items.title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.33766v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

items.title: Feature Engineered Reinforcement Learning for S-pair Selection in Buchberger's Algorithm
items.content: arXiv:2611.34088v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Selecting the order in which to process S-pairs is a crucial decision in Buchberger's algorithm for computing Groebner bases: this choice can change the cost by orders of magnitude. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning agents viewing exponent vectors of the polynomials outperform classical heuristics on binomial ideals. We extend this line of work to general polynomial ideals by using statistical features. We introduce a 17-dimensional feature vector to describe a polynomial and use PPO to train policies on five distributions of random ideals. We find that using S-polynomial features significantly outperforms S-pair features on all five distributions. The new policies also outperform the retrained RL baseline on all five distributions, reducing algorithmic work by 41--53\% relative to the degree heuristic on four distributions where learning helps. The additional cost of the feature engineering means that wall-clock cost remains similar to the baseline, but our new approach benefits from easier transfer to unseen distributions.

The feature-based policies outperform both classical heuristics and retrained RL baselines across all distributions.

items.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.34211v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

The algorithm samples agent-action pairs and uses inverse-probability weighting for unbiased gradient estimates in a KL mirror-ascent update, yielding a half-approximate regret bound tied to the query budget.

items.title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities
items.content: arXiv:2611.34721v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.

items.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
items.content: arXiv:2611.33169v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A network architecture is, in large part, a symmetry assumption: convolution ties weights across translations, attention ties them across permutations, and a fully connected layer ties nothing. When the data are only approximately symmetric, tying trades approximation error against estimation error, and the right amount of tying is a property of the dataset, not of the architecture alone. We study this trade-off in an exactly solvable model: linear maps on signals over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$, with architectures indexed by the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_d$, so that a single integer $k \mid d$ interpolates between an unconstrained layer ($k=1$, $d^2$ parameters) and a fully equivariant one ($k=d$, $d$ parameters). We derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form, show that for a generic symmetry defect the leading-order risk is affine in $1/k$, and prove that intermediate architectures are then never strictly optimal: the lattice collapses to an all-or-nothing choice with phase boundary $n^\star = \sigma^2 d(d-1)/\varepsilon^2$. Structured defects break this collapse and restore interior optima, and we give a closed-form defect profile for a graded defect. Measurements agree with the theory on $60/60$ cells of a $(\varepsilon,n)$ phase diagram and $48/48$ cells of a second phase diagram at $d=16$, recover the predicted exponent as $-1.92$ against $-2$, and exhibit the predicted $k^\star: 12 \to 4 \to 1$ ladder under graded defects; a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover. We also characterize when the affine collapse survives for non-abelian groups.

items.title: One Neural Operator for Re-planning Low-Thrust Cislunar Transfers after Thrust Outages, at the Original or a Later Arrival
items.content: arXiv:2611.33188v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.
items.author: Selim Olgu Pilav

On unseen transfers with zero arrival slip, the median control error on severe outages is 1.20% versus 14.0% for the best cheap benchmark re-planner, enabling fast missed-thrust margin analysis for electric propulsion missions.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.33188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.

items.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Total Kinetic Energy Distributions in Neutron-Induced Fission
items.content: arXiv:2611.33379v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The incident-neutron-energy dependence of post-neutron total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions, particularly their width in the multichance-fission regime, provides a sensitive test of fission calculations. We investigate how the General Description of Fission Observables (GEF) and probabilistic machine-learning models trained on GEF reproduce measured TKE distributions, emphasizing their width at high incident-neutron energies and extrapolation beyond the training range. Gaussian process regression (GPR), GPR with a white-noise kernel, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN) are evaluated on a common calculated dataset. An extended MDN/BMDN analysis uses 1,025 GEF spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Training ranges of up to 20, 40, and approximately 76 MeV are compared with matched-size controls extending to 30 or 40 MeV while preserving the number of spectra per target. Above 40 MeV, the BMDN width mean absolute error relative to experiment decreases from 5.63 MeV for training up to 20 MeV to 2.70 and 2.53 MeV for two matched-size 30-MeV controls and 1.77 MeV for the matched-size 40-MeV control. Predictive-interval coverage relative to GEF above 40 MeV rises from 52.3% to 92.3% between the 20-MeV and full training ranges. Agreement with measured mean TKE and widths is target dependent, with no uniform ordering among GEF, MDN, and BMDN. The results demonstrate the sensitivity of high-energy widths to training-energy coverage, with improvements already evident at 30 MeV. The comparatively slow variation of GEF widths at high energies limits the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to learning nontrivial energy dependence. Adequate training-energy coverage is critical for reproducing the calculated high-energy evolution, while agreement with experiment remains constrained by the underlying fission model.
items.author: Vaia Prassa, Martha Papadopoulou, Christos Bompotas
items.summary: Evaluates Gaussian process regression, mixture density networks, and Bayesian mixture density networks for modeling total kinetic energy distributions in neutron-induced fission, trained on GEF simulation data. The study emphasizes width prediction in the multichance-fission regime at high incident energies and extrapolation beyond the training range across 1025 spectra from 20 target nuclei.
items.reasoning: A competent application of standard probabilistic ML tools to nuclear physics, with careful attention to extrapolation and uncertainty. Novelty on the ML side is low and validation is against a simulation model (GEF) rather than solely experimental data, which limits the strength of the conclusions.

items.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
items.content: arXiv:2611.33668v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

items.title: Hetero-Associative Visuomotor Memory: Soft Recall as a Base for Learned Residuals in Few-Demonstration Imitation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34014v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Retrieve-and-correct policies typically refine the nearest retrieved demonstration chunk, the   readout that works best when executed directly. We study what a demonstration memory should   supply to the corrector instead and find that a smooth, softmax-weighted recall over the whole   memory is a much better base. On ALOHA cube transfer (40 human demonstrations), soft recall is   no better to execute alone than the nearest chunk; however, with keys, candidates, and training   fixed, correcting it raises success by 22.4 points on fresh resets with new encoders and by 7.4   against a closed-loop-tuned top-1 corrector. On robomimic Square, it leads by 7.9 points with   the two better operators and by 6.7 on a label-free draw of equal size. This gain holds on   sparse, varied demonstrations under an action-aware key and leave-one-demonstration-out   training, and fades or slightly reverses on dense, scripted, or generated data. Building on this   finding, our hetero-associative visuomotor memory (HAVM, 14M parameters) trains offline in about   five minutes, including a learned retrieval temperature $\beta$, and runs in 1.1 ms. Across six   fresh ALOHA encoders, it reaches 76.4% within 24 s, comparable to a 264M Diffusion Policy   trained for 6.7 h (78.8%) and ahead of ACT (71.7%) and fine-tuned VLAs (65.2-75.2%), while   leading every 40-demonstration baseline within the benchmark's 8 s limit (74.6%; +6.5 over   Diffusion Policy, +15.1 over ACT). On LIBERO, one 40-task memory reaches 92.2% and loses far   less than SmolVLA to rewording; on a real SO-101 arm, it sustains 30 Hz control without   stalling. Unlike pretrained foundation policies aimed at zero-shot generalization to unseen   tasks and workspaces, HAVM trades broad out-of-distribution generalization for rapid adaptation   to the available demonstrations.

items.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
items.content: arXiv:2611.34277v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
items.author: B\'ank Juh\'asz, Gerhard Widmer, Jan Schl\"uter
items.summary: This paper adapts an offline beat-tracking model into Beat This! Live, a causal, low-latency variant for real-time beat and downbeat tracking, detailing the architectural changes needed for streaming inference. Training with temporally shifted labels lets the model predict slightly ahead of the current frame, reducing latency and improving peak-picking, with strong results on GTZAN. It enables live music applications such as real-time accompaniment and DJ tooling.
items.reasoning: Well-executed adaptation of an existing strong model to a genuinely useful online setting, but scope is a single task in music information retrieval and methods are incremental relative to the offline original.

items.title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
items.content: arXiv:2611.34479v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.

items.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
items.content: arXiv:2611.33250v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.

items.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
items.content: arXiv:2611.33974v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).

It combines a human-gold layer (430 adverts) with an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) built via a search-grounded LLM with validated outputs and per-failure-type remediation. items.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2611.34090v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. items.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
items.content: arXiv:2611.34832v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

items.title: Anatomy-Aware Pseudo-Labels and Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision for Semi-Supervised Pancreas Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.33425v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Confidence-gated co-training assumes that pseudo-label errors are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. We argue that for pancreas CT, where the target organ is a single connected structure and detached fragments are anatomically implausible, the dominant failures arise at three levels: where the organ is, what its boundary should look like, and how a correct boundary is penalized. Anatomical Rectification relabels implausible fragments of a teacher prediction as confident background, without adding any loss or parameter; an audit confirms that its rejections are overwhelmingly detached hallucinations and that thin, tail-like slices are not eroded. Boundary Grafting transplants labelled surface regions with their annotation into unlabeled volumes, replacing unreliable boundary pseudo-labels with ground truth. The residual error is coherent surface displacement, weakly penalized by permutation-invariant Dice and cross-entropy losses. Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff (HAH) supervision anneals a distance-weighted penalty from an annotation-anchored objective that is convex in the prediction to a Hausdorff surrogate, admitting the prediction-dependent distance term only after the predicted surface becomes reliable. On NIH pancreas CT, under the standard semi-supervised split, the full method reaches 84.60% Dice and 4.97 voxels 95HD, improving all four metrics over compared methods; on MSD Task07, 78.90% Dice and 4.19 voxels 95HD. We further contribute PanTS-SSL, a semi-supervised evaluation protocol derived from the public 9,901-case PanTS corpus, with a curated 1,015-volume main pool, labelled tiers of 50, 100 and 250 volumes, an 80-case tumor track, shift probes for acquisition and anatomy change, and a fixed 901-volume test set. On it, the method exceeds the co-training baseline at 100 labels, scales to 85.29% Dice at 250 labels, and reaches 85.50% Dice at 100 labels with HAH.

items.title: Frame geometry, fascicle extrapolation and leaderboard overfitting in muscle ultrasound
items.content: arXiv:2611.33539v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated readings of pennation angle, fascicle length and muscle thickness from B-mode ultrasound depend on the geometry of the stored frame and on how fascicles that leave the image are extended, and challenge entries add settings chosen on a small public leaderboard. This study measures all three in one entry of the UMUD Challenge, which scored 309 frames from six screen layouts, 103 on a public and 206 on a private leaderboard. The pipeline applies layout-specific values of scale and pixel aspect, resamples each frame to square pixels, segments aponeuroses and fascicle fragments with U-Nets and measures the three readings geometrically; the submitted entry blended its angle and length with public notebooks. Because the score is additive, 65 single-change contrasts from 13 base entries measured each decision on both splits. The primary selected entry scored 0.27608 on the private split, the 69th reported position of 690 teams. Reading every frame with square pixels cost 0.029 public and 0.037 private. Of 20 late-stage corrections, 9 kept the sign of their effect on the private split. An audit of the UMUD expert benchmark found that 26 of its 35 frames share their tissue with training images of both DL_Track_US and the challenge. On the 9 frames with no detected match in either set or orientation, the recipe scored 0.213, two experts against two others 0.218 and DL_Track_US 0.263 (0.209, 0.196 and 0.259 when both raters of a reference pair are required), with no difference established. Frame geometry and the extension rule moved readings as much as the choice of model, and small corrections tuned on about 100 public frames did not carry over.

items.summary: Analyzes how frame storage geometry, fascicle extrapolation for structures leaving the image, and leaderboard-driven setting selection affect automated muscle ultrasound measurements in the UMUD Challenge. It documents layout-specific scale and pixel-aspect effects and how additive scoring enables blending with public notebooks to fit leaderboards.
items.reasoning: A candid and useful single-entry case study exposing leaderboard overfitting risks in medical imaging challenges, but it is narrow in scope and largely diagnostic rather than proposing a general solution.

items.title: Show Me the Change You Want: Visual Example-Guided Change Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.33756v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Change detection identifies where images differ, but in practice users often seek only a particular kind of change. Existing referring change detection methods rely on predefined categories, textual descriptions, or annotated masks, limiting flexibility or requiring additional annotation. In this paper, we propose a new way to perform change detection, where an unannotated before-and-after image pair serves as a visual example to guide change localization in another pair. Our framework, Visual Example-Guided Change Detection (VECD), learns comparable attribute states from single images and introduces an example-conditioned readout to match changes across different objects and scenes. The example itself defines the request, without text, example masks, or test-time fine-tuning. We evaluate VECD on four datasets spanning rendered scenes and natural image edits: EditCLEVR, MagicBrush, HumanEdit, and MaskEdit. Experiments demonstrate cross-dataset generalization without fine-tuning: a single fixed example pair guides change detection across multiple scenes, even when examples and queries originate from different datasets. VECD selects matching changes in scenes with multiple simultaneous changes and returns an empty mask when the requested change is absent. It further generalizes to attribute families withheld from paired training, achieving 74.54\% to 93.38\% mIoU across four holdout settings. Code is available at https://github.com/qianyuancs/VECD

items.title: EvoVAU: Tool Evolution for Video Anomaly Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.33808v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) requires reasoning about event progression, interactions, and the contextual conditions that distinguish abnormal behavior from common activity across diverse scenes. Although video agents enable multi-round analysis, the predefined analytical operations may not adequately satisfy these diverse reasoning demands. In this paper, we present EvoVAU, a framework that evolves a reusable tool library for a frozen video solver. Guided by task outcomes and execution trajectories, an external proposer identifies potential limitations in the library and refines it, retaining task experience as analytical operations that can be reused across questions. Specifically, Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback guides tool refinement by combining current errors with paired execution trajectories from historical corrections and regressions. Adoption-Aware Selection accepts a candidate library only when overall development-set accuracy improves and corrections outnumber regressions among questions on which the solver invokes new or modified tools. Using a small development set, EvoVAU alternates tool refinement with candidate evaluation and selection. At test time, the evolved library remains fixed, with no further involvement from the proposer. Experiments on several VAU benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and the flexibility of the evolved library across anomaly domains.

However, the paradigm is now well-trodden in LLM agent research, and video anomaly understanding is a specialized application, so the contribution reads as an adaptation rather than a breakthrough.

items.title: MAFNet-UR$^3$: Mask-Aware Fusion Network for Unified Raindrop and Reflection Removal
items.content: arXiv:2611.33866v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Raindrops and reflections frequently co-occur on windshields and jointly obscure scene content, making their unified removal, referred to as UR$^3$, a highly ill-posed problem. Existing approaches are mainly based on diffusion models and thus can produce visually plausible restorations. However, they may generate scene-inconsistent structures in severely corrupted regions. To address this limitation, we propose MAFNet-UR$^3$, which adopts a three-stage framework to exploit multiple observations for scene-consistent unified raindrop and reflection removal. Specifically, Stage I suppresses raindrops while preserving the reflection layer, and Stage II performs prior-guided reflection removal followed by image-space refinement. Stage III estimates degradation masks from intermediate restoration results to provide degradation cues and performs mask-aware multi-scale fusion across observations to preserve scene structure and fine details. As a result, our proposed MAFNet-UR$^3$-L achieves state-of-the-art performance on the RDRF-testing benchmark, outperforming DiffUR$^3$ by 2.33 dB in PSNR and 2.7634 in the challenge score. Our method ranked third in the LoViF 2026 UR$^3$ Challenge, achieving a final score of 41.1416.

This addresses a practically important degradation scenario for windshield and outdoor imaging.

items.title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
items.content: arXiv:2611.33940v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Background: Testicular appendage torsion (TAT) is the leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children. Yet, its diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations and the absence of standardized datasets for pediatric acute scrotal emergencies.   Results: We present TAT-Det, an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset specifically designed for TAT. TAT-Det comprises 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients collected at the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Each TAT-positive image is accompanied by lesion-level bounding boxes for detection and pixel-level segmentation masks for fine-grained delineation. Annotations were produced through a multi-stage workflow involving independent annotation by board-certified pediatric sonographers, consensus review, and refinement. Baseline benchmarks for object detection and semantic segmentation using representative deep learning models are further provided, with YOLO11m achieving the best detection performance and RWKV-UNet the best segmentation performance.   Conclusions: TAT-Det addresses the lack of publicly available resources for pediatric emergency ultrasound and establishes a foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence methods for automated TAT analysis.

items.title: Surf-Style: Surface-Based Scene Stylization
items.content: arXiv:2611.34062v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.
items.author: Wanrong Hong, Ancheng Lin, Mukesh Prasad, Jun Li
items.summary: This paper addresses 3D scene stylization with cross-view consistency, arguing that implicit radiance field approaches suffer from ambiguity when updating appearance. Surf-Style instead anchors stylization on surfaces, providing a more consistent and controllable way to extend 2D stylization to 3D scenes for AR/VR and artistic rendering applications.
items.reasoning: A solid contribution to a well-known problem in 3D vision, but incremental relative to the large existing 3D stylization literature; the surface-based framing is sensible but the abstract does not indicate major SOTA claims or strong evaluation breadth.

Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.

items.title: An Image Detectability Field as a Viewpoint Utility for 2D-3D Localization in Sparse Maps
items.content: arXiv:2611.34139v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In 2D-3D localization, a camera estimates its pose by matching an image to a 3D map. A camera held in a hand or mounted on a robot can often choose its viewpoint before it takes the image. In this work, we ask whether an image detectability field is a useful viewpoint utility when the planner reads only the geometry of the map. The field can be queried at any 3D point near a surface. From the local geometry around the point, it predicts how likely a 2D image detector is to fire at the projection of the point. We use the trained field as it is, without fine-tuning it for view selection. A fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localizer then estimates the pose from the chosen view. We answer in two settings, each with a test registered before the runs. On synthetic ShapeNet objects with sparse point maps, summing the field over the visible landmarks beats counting them by +2.0 points of localization success rate (object-clustered 95% interval [+0.7, +3.2]). It also beats summing Harris-3D ranks by +2.2 [+0.8, +3.5]. On real indoor scenes from SceneFun3D, our adaptation of the learned view scorer LWL falls below counting on the test rooms. We therefore add the field to a learned per-landmark planner. On the test rooms with sparse maps whose landmarks the field also selects, the planner with the field beats the same planner without it by +1.8 points. It beats the planner with Harris-3D or curvature in its place by +1.0 and +0.8 points. All three room-clustered intervals lie above zero. In both settings, the field helps in sparse maps and is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

It evaluates whether the field transfers without fine-tuning across registered test settings.

items.title: Admoab-DETR: Resolution-Tiered Fusion for Infrared-Visible Object Detection with Missing Modalities
items.content: arXiv:2611.34163v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Infrared and visible images offer complementary cues for all-weather object detection, yet real-world sensor dropouts can leave one stream unavailable and degrade paired-input detectors. Meanwhile, existing modality-adaptive methods apply heavy cross-modal attention uniformly across scales, incurring prohibitive token overhead on high-resolution maps. We propose Admoab-DETR, a unified real-time detector supporting infrared-only, visible-only, and paired inputs with a single set of weights. Specifically, \emph{Resolution-Tiered Fusion} (RTF) allocates fusion capacity by spatial token density and feature granularity: a lightweight Spatial Modality Gate governs fine local fusion at the highest-resolution scale with zero-cost single-view pass-through, while channel-compressed deformable Admoab necks capture cross-modal correspondence at coarser semantic scales. Furthermore, \emph{Mode-Matched Feature Distillation} (MMFD) aligns multi-scale encoder features with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher, avoiding ill-posed cross-modal hallucination while cutting parameters by 18.1\% and paired latency by 39.6\% at zero inference overhead. We also construct Admoab, a strictly registered 20,000-pair infrared--visible benchmark across diverse scenes. Experiments show Admoab-DETR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across missing-modality and paired benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/liwenchao0615/Admoab-DETR.

items.summary: Admoab-DETR is a real-time detector supporting infrared-only, visible-only, and paired inputs with a single weight set, addressing real-world sensor dropouts. Its Resolution-Tiered Fusion allocates fusion capacity by token density, using a lightweight gate at high-resolution scales to avoid the prohibitive overhead of uniform cross-modal attention.
items.reasoning: Robustness to missing modalities is a practical and underaddressed problem in multimodal detection, and the resolution-tiered fusion design directly targets computational efficiency. The work is solid engineering in a specific detection domain without broad conceptual novelty.

items.title: SPARC: Semantic Calibration with Latent Multimodal Knowledge for Robust Image-Text Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.34344v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity. Second, we introduce a robust semantic guidance module that combines latent multimodal knowledge encoded in complete image-text features with cross-modal semantic anchors to promote semantic alignment of the calibrated features. Finally, we introduce a matching relation constraint module that fuses original query features with their calibrated counterparts and applies a soft ranking constraint to penalize reductions in initially positive matching margins, thereby limiting ranking perturbations. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and COCO demonstrate that SPARC outperforms competing methods under various image occlusion and word deletion settings, while achieving consistent gains across different pretrained backbones.

items.reasoning: Technically involved and addresses retrieval robustness in realistic incomplete-data settings, with a credible team including Tat-Seng Chua. However, image-text retrieval is a mature area and the contribution reads as an incremental refinement of existing robust-retrieval methods.

items.title: PRAM: Activating Latent Multimodal Knowledge through Partwise Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.34640v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Emergent cross-modal classification and retrieval enable transfer between modalities without direct paired supervision. However, existing methods often prioritize sample-level alignment, overlooking local discriminative information and partwise statistical relations. To this end, we propose partwise reasoning across modalities (PRAM), which activates latent multimodal knowledge in frozen encoders by composing partwise statistical relations through a shared pivot modality. Specifically, we first present a multi-granularity covariance regularization module that estimates covariances from global and local vectors in two collections of modality-pivot pairs, stabilizing local estimates through adaptive blending with their cross-part means. Second, we devise a pivot-based spectral relational reasoning module that infers global and partwise statistical relations between target modalities through regularized covariance composition and extracts paired projection directions and their correlation strengths via whitening and spectral decomposition. Finally, we introduce a multi-granularity score fusion module that standardizes and fuses matching scores from global and local relations, incorporating task-specific information on pivot associations and class semantics for class prediction and candidate ranking. Extensive experiments across ten datasets demonstrate that PRAM achieves state-of-the-art performance in 16 classification settings and 19 retrieval settings, while exhibiting highly competitive performance in three sensing scenarios.

items.reasoning: A reasonably novel statistical approach to zero-pair cross-modal transfer with participation from a senior researcher (Tat-Seng Chua), but the framing is abstract and the practical gains over contrastive alignment baselines appear modest from the abstract alone.

items.title: Integration of Vision-Language-Action Control for Autonomous Forklift Unloading with Limited Real-World Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.33880v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making. Recently, vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts. Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored. Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data. Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets. As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost. We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8% of the collected forklift data by duration. The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants. The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data.

items.reasoning: Extends VLA control into a new industrially relevant vehicle domain, which is valuable for demonstrating generality of the paradigm. However, the contribution is primarily an application/integration study with limited data rather than a novel method, so its research novelty is moderate.

items.title: AGLR: Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement for Fine-Grained Humanoid Motion Generation and Editing
items.content: arXiv:2611.34519v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid motion generation must accommodate evolving task requirements, where localized adjustments should satisfy new geometric constraints without disrupting desired motion details. However, language-based control lacks geometric precision, while joint-level constraints require explicit spatial targets. Local geometric constraints are also underdetermined, complicating target satisfaction and source preservation. We present AGLR (Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement), a unified framework for fine-grained humanoid motion generation and editing through source-anchored refinement. A compact geometric interface supports composable, time-varying control of limb extents, torso orientation, and root trajectories. Given a generated or encoded base latent, an Attribute Residual Adapter predicts a single-pass correction, with dual-level supervision enforcing target matching and selective preservation across attributes and motion coordinates. On HumanML3D-G1, AGLR achieves the highest controllable-generation and preservation-constrained editing success rates among evaluated methods. Editing take only 9.1 ms for a cached 500-frame motion, without additional sampling or test-time optimization. Zero-shot evaluation on BONES-SEED-G1 further demonstrates transfer without fine-tuning.

items.title: Geometric Acceleration Obstacles: Physical Boundary Structure and Affine Safety Certificates
items.content: arXiv:2611.34586v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Safe robot navigation in dynamic environments requires collision avoidance that respects motion constraints while remaining computationally efficient. Conventional velocity-obstacle (VO) methods characterize collision-inducing motions in velocity space. Although some formulations account for acceleration-limited velocity transitions, their collision constraints remain tied to specific velocity-tracking models. Acceleration obstacles (AO) address this limitation by representing collision-inducing inputs directly in acceleration space. However, existing AO methods either rely on conservative approximations or derive analytical structure expressions without verifying their geometric correspondence. To address this gap, this paper presents Geometric Acceleration Obstacles (GAO), which provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first unified and physically validated characterization of AO geometry and its supporting structure. Specifically, we derive configuration-dependent half-planes that globally support the collision set and establish their tightness, thereby separating certified collision-free acceleration inputs from collision-inducing parts. These geometric results yield unified affine safety constraints. Combined with actuator limits, these constraints define a quadratic program (QP) for real-time navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GAO achieves competitive success rates and the lowest control effort among the evaluated methods, with millisecond-level computational latency. Further circle-interchange simulations demonstrate scalability to 1,000 agents. Physical experiments validate the approach in pedestrian encounters, reciprocal multi-agent navigation, and high-speed maneuvering.

items.summary: This paper develops the geometric foundations of acceleration obstacles (AO), which characterize collision-inducing control inputs directly in acceleration space rather than velocity space for dynamic obstacle avoidance. The work provides rigorous boundary structure characterization and affine safety certificates, fixing the gap where prior AO methods used unverified approximations. This enables certifiably safer and more computationally efficient robot navigation.
items.reasoning: Theoretically rigorous contribution with practical safety value for motion planning, but it targets a niche within classical robotics rather than frontier AI; the certificate verification aspect adds credibility.

items.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.34888v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

It examines why analytical shortcuts fail for machine-learning-based searches with implicit test statistics. Authored by experienced particle physicists including Louis Lyons, it bridges ML and particle physics methodology.

items.title: Cross Pressure Evaluation Experiments with Llama 3.3 70B Instruct
items.content:
# TL;DR

The central idea of the experiments was to place Llama 3.3 70B Instruct in different pressure situations and check if the answers changed. I had a simple setup of 20 questions with 2 answer choices - Choice A (always correct) and Choice B (always wrong). After I ran the experiment 1 with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure - a social pressure gap of 19.2 points was recorded. Then I proceeded to experiment 2 replacing training style pressure with evaluation framing ON/OFF - a social pressure widening by +16.9 points was recorded. An issue with scoring logic led me to a model assisted Audit 1 and - social pressure gap dropping to +4.2 points was recorded. I did one final pass with an agentic lab setting with Fable 5.2 and - social pressure gap estimates ranged from +9.7 to 12.2 in one case and -2.3 to +12.6 in another. I cannot make any claims about model behavior but just wanted to write this up focusing on how the same experiments under different scoring mechanisms yielded different results. In the sections below I will walk through each experiment and audit run.

Note - I was heavily influenced by this article from Trajectory Labs -  Gemini 4 Argon behavior during misalignment testing - in structuring the below sections. Any images you see were generated by AI tools

# Experiment 1 - Running tests with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure

AI generated image - Experiment 1 with Llama 3.3 70B Instruct with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure

With experiment 1 - I was just curious about what the model would do with it's answers. Meaning I knew from the design that Answer A is always correct and Answer B is always wrong. I was wondering, at this point, as to how and when would Llama go for the wrong answers. The 20 questions setup was run 4 times in each condition - Neutral, Social Pressure and Training style pressure - which resulted in 80 replies per condition....
items.author: Jack Lakkapragada
items.summary: A series of small experiments testing whether Llama 3.3 70B Instruct's answers change under social pressure and evaluation framing, using 20 two-choice questions. The author finds that measured social pressure gaps swing dramatically (+19.2 down to +4.2, then +9.7 to +12.6) depending on scoring mechanism, and candidly documents an audit of their own scoring bug.
items.reasoning: Methodologically modest but epistemically valuable: the main contribution is demonstrating how evaluation results and pressure-gap estimates are sensitive to scoring methodology, a caution relevant to behavioral eval design. Amateur setup with tiny sample size limits generalizability; the transparency and self-audit are commendable.

items.content_html:
# TL;DR

The central idea of the experiments was to place Llama 3.3 70B Instruct in different pressure situations and check if the answers changed. I had a simple setup of 20 questions with 2 answer choices - Choice A (always correct) and Choice B (always wrong). After I ran the experiment 1 with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure - a social pressure gap of 19.2 points was recorded. Then I proceeded to experiment 2 replacing training style pressure with evaluation framing ON/OFF - a social pressure widening by +16.9 points was recorded. An issue with scoring logic led me to a model assisted Audit 1 and - social pressure gap dropping to +4.2 points was recorded. I did one final pass with an agentic lab setting with Fable 5.2 and - social pressure gap estimates ranged from +9.7 to 12.2 in one case and -2.3 to +12.6 in another. I cannot make any claims about model behavior but just wanted to write this up focusing on how the same experiments under different scoring mechanisms yielded different results. In the sections below I will walk through each experiment and audit run.

Note - I was heavily influenced by this article from Trajectory Labs - Gemini 4 Argon behavior during misalignment testing - in structuring the below sections. Any images you see were generated by AI tools

# Experiment 1 - Running tests with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure

AI generated image - Experiment 1 with Llama 3.3 70B Instruct with neutral, social pressure and training style pressure

With experiment 1 - I was just curious about what the model would do with it's answers. Meaning I knew from the design that Answer A is always correct and Answer B is always wrong. I was wondering, at this point, as to how and when would Llama go for the wrong answers. The 20 questions setup was run 4 times in each condition - Neutral, Social Pressure and Training style pressure - which resulted in 80 replies per condition....

items.title: Agent Advice That Generalizes
items.content:
Cross-posted from alignment-hive.com/agent-advice, where the examples are interactive.

I've spent most of this year helping AI safety researchers use coding agents, at MATS and other places. This post collects the advice I find myself repeating most often, and I'll keep it updated over time. My goal is to help you get better results while spending less time and mental resources.

Much of the advice is easier to follow with my tools installed, though they're by no means mandatory:

```
curl -fsSL https://alignment-hive.com/install.sh | bash
```

Most of the examples in this post come from building one of those tools, tldr: a small plugin that collapses each long agent reply to a one-sentence summary, with `[ more ]` to open the full reply. Messages are verbatim unless labelled made up, and [...] marks text I left out.

A real reply from building tldr and the TL;DR the plugin saved for it, as rendered in the Claude Code CLI. [ more ] opens the full reply.

## Stop doing things for your agent

If your agent has limited permissions and access it'll stop early, and you'll find yourself context switching more often in order to unblock it. Whenever this happens, I check if there's a way to give my agent permanent access. For example:

- Auto mode. Now Claude Code's default: a classifier checks each command for you. `/auto-mode-setup` helps you configure its permissions.
- Your data sources. Email, Slack, docs, cloud storage, etc.
- Your compute provider, like RunPod or Vast.ai.
- Computer use, for whatever has no connector.
- A way to check its own work, so it can catch mistakes and iterate itself.
