items.title: Hopkins Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity Post-Event Report
items.content:
JHU AI Safety and Biosecurity (ASBS) recently hosted our inaugural event “Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity.” Much thanks to BlueDot Impact for making this financially possible through Rapid Grants and to partner organizations, the HLTCOE, HopAI, and Rosetta Commons.

Quick rundown:

- 105 RSVP
- 85 attendees
- 4 talks: Biosecurity in the Age of AI (Dr. Jeffrey Gray) Loss of Control Risks and the Hugging Face Incident (Dr. William Walden) Mental Models and Foundations of AI Safety (Jonathan Ouyang) Takeoffs and Timelines (Malcolm Krolick)

Takeaways and learning:

- Low poll response rate (27%) as QR code wasn’t up long enough
- Event ran slightly too long, so ending poll + recruitment slides didn’t hit full room
- Explain the two-poll structure, as there seemed to be confusion about the goal of the polls

Poll questions (identical before and after event)

- What is the likelihood of AI ending humanity?
- What year do you think it'll happen? (answer N/A if you put 0%)

Results:

Average p(doom) among paired poll responders went from 50% to 59% (excluding 3 potential COIs, 47% → 57%):

58% increased their estimate, 42% reported no change, and 0% decreased it (sign test, p = 0.016); the largest individual increase was 40 percentage points (from 10% to 50%).

The predicted year tended to move earlier:

although this was not statistically significant due to low statistical power.

Seven people joined ASBS on the day of the event and nine within the week, compared with two the week before (one-sided binomial test, p = 0.033):

Overall, it seems that people were broadly interested and informed by the talks, but the call-to-action barrier was still somewhat high. It’s really hard to say anything quantitative about these results given the selection biases and low response rates/statistical power, but directionally it seems reasonable. Would love to know if these results are similar to other people’s experiences, and to get advice on future events!

Pre/post polls showed average p(doom) rising from about 50% to 59%, with zero respondents decreasing their estimate.
items.reasoning: Modest but concrete field-building data point: documented outreach outcomes from a university safety group, including self-reported belief shifts, with appropriate caveats about small samples, polling mechanics, and self-selection. items.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.34942v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

items.title: Gradient TD($\lambda$) for Non-Linear Function Approximation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34826v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Temporal difference (TD) learning is central to reinforcement learning. Many methods use semi-gradient TD, which may diverge, or develop algorithms with mean-squared Bellman or TD-error objectives that are difficult to analyze. Gradient TD algorithms overcome these challenges by using projection of the value function and present convergent off-policy algorithms. However, the algorithm for $\lambda$-return was limited to linear function approximation. Here, we extend the same to non-linear function approximation, which is desirable since many strong modern function approximators are complex and non-linear. Recent works have derived similar algorithms with a generalized projected Bellman error objective. Alternatively, we continue working with the projected Bellman error.
items.author: Sujeet Lahane
items.summary: This paper extends gradient TD algorithms for lambda-returns from linear to non-linear function approximation, continuing to work with the projection-based approach to retain convergence guarantees for off-policy learning. This addresses the divergence issues of semi-gradient TD when using modern complex function approximators.
items.reasoning: Useful extension of classical TD convergence theory to non-linear approximation, relevant as modern approximators are non-linear, but the abstract notes similar algorithms have recently been derived via generalized projected Bellman error objectives, tempering novelty.

items.title: Sliding-Window Detection of Hidden Regimes under Stochastic Switching
items.content: arXiv:2611.34905v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A sliding-window average is a simple estimator of the current state of a hidden regime-switching process, such as a hidden Markov model. A longer window averages out more noise but is more likely to contain a switch, and the question is what such a switch costs. We analyse the decoder that assigns the average of the last $m$ observations to the nearest regime mean. For two regimes with conditionally independent, stochastically ordered observations, a switch inside the window, averaged uniformly over its positions and directions, causes an error with probability exactly $1/2$. Consequently, for every stationary switching law, the error is at most $\bar P(m)+\bar s(m-1)/2$, where $\bar P(m)$ is the stationary-weighted single-regime error and $\bar s$ the switch rate. Under Markov switching, time reversal shows that a window whose oldest and current regimes differ is misclassified with probability exactly $1/2$, however many switches it contains, and the bound is attained up to a factor $p_{\min}^{m-1}$. For Gaussian noise with common variance, minimizing the bound gives an explicit window length which, in units of $\sigma^2/\Delta^2$, depends only on the expected number of switches in that time. As switching probabilities vanish proportionally, the optimal error is $\bar s\log(1/\bar s)/(2I)(1+o(1))$, with $I$ the single-regime Chernoff exponent. In the Gaussian case this is twice the Bayes error. For symmetric switching, exponentially weighted moving averages reduce this factor to at most $2\log2\approx1.39$, and two-block weights adapted to the switch rate attain the Bayes rate. For three or more regimes, long-window switch costs are set by the geometry of the regime means. For Markov-modulated random walks with $\pm1$ steps on a reflecting lattice, a position-aware decoder learns as fast as without walls under holding boundaries, while steps at bouncing boundaries carry none.
items.author: Arina Pambukyan, Hayk Nersisyan
items.summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the simple nearest-mean decoder applied to sliding-window averages of a hidden regime-switching process, deriving an exact result that a switch inside the window causes error with probability exactly 1/2 under stated conditions. This yields a clean error bound decomposing single-regime error plus a switching penalty term. It quantifies the bias-variance-like tradeoff of window length for regime detection.
items.reasoning: Elegant and exact theoretical result for a simple estimator, but the scope is narrow (two regimes, specific conditions) and the practical implications for modern ML are limited; good craftsmanship in a small corner of sequential analysis.

items.title: UniMoE-CP: Unified Conditional Waveform Prediction Across Measured Optical Wireless Links
items.content: arXiv:2611.33198v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Shared prediction across measured optical wireless links requires a common model to accommodate link-dependent waveform dynamics. This paper studies unified learning for underwater optical, 100-m visible-light communication and 4.3-km free-space optical links. We formulate received-waveform forecasting from historical observations and known future transmitted excitation using one shared parameter set. UniMoE-CP combines a shared pool of temporal experts, window-dependent routing and spectral covariate fusion with an autoregressive decoder. The design permits conditional specialization while reusing expert parameters across the measured links. Pooled-training benchmarks evaluate each link separately and report an aggregated result using normalized mean square error (NMSE) and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE). The reported average NMSE reductions are 29.9% for 100-m VLC, 29.1% underwater and 21.4% for 4.3-km FSO. The aggregated average NMSE decreases from 0.1645 for the best baseline to 0.1178 for UniMoE-CP.

It enables conditional specialization while reusing expert parameters across measured links.

items.title: InterConRank: Joint Node Centrality in Interconnected Heterogeneous Networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.34763v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Two nodes with identical connections within their own layer can differ in importance if their neighbors in another layer occupy different positions in the network. We introduce InterConRank, a centrality algorithm that computes a separate node ranking for each layer of an interconnected network. Directed dependencies specify which layers supply scores to each receiving layer. InterConRank normalizes each type of link separately and updates all layers together, so a score can cross into a layer in one iteration and propagate along its internal links in the next. We prove convergence of this joint update and evaluate the resulting rankings on four scholarly networks. On all four networks, InterConRank gives the highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations for nodes in the collaboration layer.

items.summary: This paper introduces InterConRank, a centrality algorithm that computes per-layer node rankings in interconnected heterogeneous networks, where a node's importance in one layer depends on its neighbors' positions in other layers. items.title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.34870v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

items.title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
items.content: arXiv:2611.33332v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.

items.title: Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.34527v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.

items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-UAV Data Harvesting Under Variable Team Sizes and Agent Loss
items.content: arXiv:2611.34818v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.

items.summary: The paper proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible MADDPG variant enabling decentralized multi-UAV teams to harvest data from wireless sensors under varying team sizes and agent failures, avoiding costly per-population policy retraining. This improves robustness of learned coordination policies when UAVs drop out during missions.
items.reasoning: Useful robotics/coordination contribution addressing agent loss in MARL, but the approach is an incremental variant of an established algorithm applied to a specific scenario.

items.title: A Hard Background Pairing Transfers across Classifiers and Images
items.content: arXiv:2611.34645v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: An image classifier names the object in an image, and its accuracy is the share of images named correctly. A classifier that names a car on a road may miss the same car pasted onto clouds. Composite benchmarks measure such failures by pasting objects cut from photographs onto backgrounds from other photographs. A pairing puts every object label on a different background label, such as truck on sea. The pairing on which some classifiers do worst, their hardest pairing, makes a strict test, but may be hard only for them or only on the photographs used to choose it. We show that the hardest pairing of some classifiers stays hard for others and on new photographs. We split 40 ImageNet classifiers into halves balanced by reported ImageNet accuracy. One half picks its hardest pairing of 8 object and 8 background labels from Common Objects in Context (COCO). The other half, held out of the choice, compares that pairing with random pairings of the same objects and backgrounds. For the 14 held-out classifiers with little net accuracy change after pasting objects back onto their own backgrounds, mean accuracy on composites from new photographs falls from 50.3% over random pairings to 43.7% on the hardest pairing, 6.6 percentage points lower. A benchmark using these composites can compare this pool's held-out classifiers on the fixed and random pairings.
items.author: Karl Li
items.summary: Studying composite benchmarks where objects are pasted onto mismatched backgrounds, the paper shows that the background pairing on which some ImageNet classifiers perform worst remains hard for other classifiers and on new photographs. Splitting 40 ImageNet classifiers into accuracy-balanced halves, the authors demonstrate that context-failure difficulty is a property of the pairing itself rather than idiosyncratic to particular models or images. This has implications for constructing robust stress tests of visual context dependence.
items.reasoning: Interesting, cleanly designed finding about transferability of background-induced failure modes, but the single-author scope and ImageNet-classifier-only setting limit the breadth of conclusions.

items.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
items.content: arXiv:2611.34137v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.
items.author: Jacques Savoy
items.summary: This short paper improves the classic Delta authorship attribution method by applying a resampling procedure to selected stylistic features, increasing accuracy while preserving the interpretability of results based on most-frequent words. The main cost is additional computation time. It is a focused methodological refinement of a widely used stylometry baseline.
items.reasoning: A modest but honest incremental improvement to an established method; useful for stylometry practitioners, though the technique and evaluation scale offer limited novelty.

items.title: A Calibration-Referenced Protocol for Measuring Decision Stability under Reference Bank Compression
items.content: arXiv:2611.34134v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reference banks used for industrial image inspection can be compressed to fit a deployment budget, but the resulting anomaly decisions depend on both the compressed scores and the operating threshold. We present a four-step protocol that compares compression methods at matched deployment sizes, establishes a reference distribution from 200 recalibrations, evaluates disagreement against two calibration benchmarks, and measures changes by distance from the full-bank threshold. With WideResNet-50, budget-matched product quantization (PQ) at the 10% budget has the lowest decision disagreement among five matched methods, including int8 scalar quantization, on VisA and MVTec AD at both operating levels. Int8 scalar quantization gives lower disagreement than PQ at the other four budgets. On MVTec AD at the lower operating level, PQ meets the calibration median in 34/39 cells and the upper quantile in 39/39 cells. Category-equally weighted image-level AUROC loss at this budget ranges from 0.0003 to 0.0037 across the evaluated configurations. On VisA at the 1% budget and a 1% operating level, disagreement reaches 28.12% (95% CI 23.25--33.58%) among near-threshold anomalies and 1.30% (0.79--2.14%) across the normal holdout. The 10% budget-matched PQ setting retains the lowest disagreement among four compared methods with ResNet-18, with clean reference banks, and when thresholds are estimated from normal-directory probes. The protocol connects deployment size to a calibration-referenced decision measure and identifies the evaluation populations most informative for inspection.

items.summary: This paper proposes a four-step protocol for fairly comparing reference-bank compression methods in industrial anomaly inspection at matched deployment budgets, using recalibration-based reference distributions and threshold-distance analysis. Empirically, budget-matched product quantization at a 10% budget shows the lowest decision disagreement among five methods on VisA and MVTec AD.
items.reasoning: A careful measurement-protocol contribution for a narrow industrial deployment problem. The methodology is sound and practically useful for practitioners, but the scope and general interest are limited.

items.title: Real-time Food Recipe Generation with Mobile Deep Learning and Large Language Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.33177v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Finding recipes that match available kitchen ingredients can be cumbersome and inefficient. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a mobile application that generates tailored food recipes based on ingredients identified using a mobile camera. Leveraging deep learning and large language model (LLM), our system offers a seamless and efficient solution for real-time recipe generation. By integrating deep learning for accurate ingredient recognition with LLM for generating detailed and practical recipes, our approach ensures users receive precise cooking instructions based on actual ingredients on hand. Extensive dataset augmentation and model training have resulted in a robust system capable of high performance. Experimental results demonstrate that EfficientNet, used for food recognition, offers a balance of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it ideal for mobile applications. This dual-approach method enhances the cooking experience, reduces food waste, and provides a comprehensive, real-time tool for everyday cooking needs, bridging a significant gap in current food recommendation systems.

items.title: Is Chaotic Dynamics Enhancing Particle Swarm Optimization? An Anytime Performance Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.34692v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The search dynamics of particle swarm optimization (PSO) can be driven by random or chaotic values. We study if there are performance differences between random and chaos if distributional equivalence of the used sequences is observed. Therefore, we consider an anytime performance assessment which quantifies the fraction of runs reaching a given target value within a specified numerical budget. Furthermore, we connect quantifiers of the chaotic dynamics to performance metrics of the anytime analysis. The results show that once the underlying distributions are controlled, deterministic chaotic sequences yield no general or consistent advantage over random sequences. Performance differences arise most prominently from the underlying distribution, but also from search-space dimensions, benchmark targets, and numerical budgets. We also find potential budget-dependent advantages under specific parametrization of chaotic maps and distribution settings.
items.author: Hendrik Richter
items.summary: This study asks whether deterministic chaotic drive sequences improve particle swarm optimization compared to random sequences when distributional equivalence is enforced, using an anytime performance assessment tied to run-budgets. The main finding is a negative one: once underlying distributions are controlled, chaos provides no general or consistent advantage, with observed differences attributable to distributional properties. This debunks a recurring claim in the PSO literature with a careful controlled design.
items.reasoning: Methodologically valuable as a rigorous negative result that corrects a common confounded comparison, but negative findings in a niche algorithmic subfield have limited impact. The anytime assessment framing is a nice contribution to evaluation practice.

items.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
items.content: arXiv:2611.33702v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

items.summary: This is a cross-listed comparative study of two small biologically inspired hexapedal robots (DASH and RoACH) on rigid versus flowing substrates, varying ground properties and stride frequency to measure speed, power, and cost of transport. It aims to build the ground-interaction models needed to design robots that locomote over yielding, granular terrain. The work is foundational terradynamics from well-known groups (Goldman, Fearing, Li).

items.title: How to prove a counterfactual in space pizza court
items.content:
To reason through decisions, an agent considers possibilities like: if I do this, the result will be that.
If I take this route, it will take me 15 minutes to deliver this pizza, but if I take that route, it will take an hour.

These are counterfactual conditionals.
If the agent takes the shorter route, we have a false antecedent in "if I had taken the longer one, it would have taken an hour".
There is no way to compare such counterfactuals to reality.
If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible.

I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood.
The name should have been a warning, but I ordered from them because they guarantee the shortest possible route.
When the pizza took an hour to arrive, I took SophistBot to court over this guarantee, which shows you how seriously we take pizza out here in the asteroid belt.

My claim to the judge: if SophistBot had taken the shortest route, my pizza would have arrived in 15 minutes.
I even had the route in hand.
SophistBot's response: their route, which took an hour, was better than my supposed "shortest route".
In fact, they claimed to believe that my "so-called 'shortest route'" would have taken six hours.

SophistBot explained to the court that if they had taken my "controversial route", as they now took to calling it, then we would have seen whether it truly takes 15 minutes or six hours.
But, they did not, so it was simply a matter of opinion.

Absurd—because in the asteroid belt, delivery times are perfectly predictable.
Delivery robots do not drive pizza to its destination, but launch it....
items.author: transhumanist_atom_understander
items.summary: A whimsical dialogic thought experiment in which the author sues a space-station pizzeria over a shortest-route guarantee, using the scenario to explore how counterfactual conditionals can be evidenced when the antecedent is logically impossible for a deterministic agent. It connects the pedagogy to decision theory and agent reasoning about counterfactuals.
items.reasoning: Accessible and entertaining decision-theory pedagogy on a genuinely subtle topic—evidence for counterfactuals in deterministic settings—relevant to AI decision theory discussions. It is exposition through fiction rather than original theory, so moderate value.

If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible.

I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood.

The name should have been a warning, but I ordered from them because they guarantee the shortest possible route.

When the pizza took an hour to arrive, I took SophistBot to court over this guarantee, which shows you how seriously we take pizza out here in the asteroid belt.

My claim to the judge: if SophistBot had taken the shortest route, my pizza would have arrived in 15 minutes.

I even had the route in hand.

SophistBot's response: their route, which took an hour, was better than my supposed "shortest route".

In fact, they claimed to believe that my "so-called 'shortest route'" would have taken six hours.

SophistBot explained to the court that if they had taken my "controversial route", as they now took to calling it, then we would have seen whether it truly takes 15 minutes or six hours.

But, they did not, so it was simply a matter of opinion.

Absurd—because in the asteroid belt, delivery times are perfectly predictable.

Delivery robots do not drive pizza to its destination, but launch it....

items.title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.33411v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.

items.title: ChemoMAE: Self-Supervised Spectral Representation Learning Reveals Chemical Heterogeneity in Historical Wood
items.content: arXiv:2611.34581v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In historical timber buildings, multiple environmental factors act over centuries on wood whose chemical composition varies across anatomical regions, producing complex patterns of degradation. Understanding how timber members degrade is important for the effective conservation and restoration of historical buildings, yet the mechanisms underlying these patterns remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we used self-supervised learning to establish a common basis for comparing specimens from timber members that differ in wood species and service history. We examined transverse sections of 49 wood specimens from several historical buildings in Japan using near-infrared hyperspectral imaging. ChemoMAE, a self-supervised Transformer, learns pixelwise spectral representations through masked denoising that exploits multicollinearity among spectral variables. Clustering these representations yields spatial maps without predefined chemical-state categories. Because anatomy and degradation can produce spatially continuous regions, we formulated Local Label Agreement (LLA) to quantify agreement among labels assigned to neighboring pixels. Using spectra alone, ChemoMAE yielded higher mean LLA than baseline methods on validation specimens. We then trained ChemoMAE anew and fitted cluster centers across all specimens. Spatial structures consistent with wood anatomy and the expected effects of surface exposure emerged in the resulting maps. By cross-referencing regional spectra and spatial distributions across specimens in light of wood anatomy, service histories, and prior studies, we proposed models of internal and surface degradation as mechanistic hypotheses. This exploratory AI for Science framework gives researchers a basis for linking latent patterns learned through self-supervision with domain knowledge when investigating how material states form.

items.title: Evaluating Aviation Safety Knowledge Extraction with SmolLM2: From Zero-Shot to Retrieval-Grounded Prompting
items.content: arXiv:2611.34432v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Aviation accident narratives contain safety knowledge that is difficult to capture using structured occurrence fields alone. This study evaluates prompting-based knowledge extraction across four dimensions: concept accuracy, verbatim evidence grounding, structural compliance, and directed relation extraction. SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct was evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting using 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives from 2000-2020, containing 3,763 reference concepts and 467 directed relations. Evaluation combined structural checks, verbatim evidence matching, expert-reviewed semantic matching, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. No prompting strategy performed best across all dimensions. Retrieval-grounded prompting achieved the highest concept micro-F1 of 32.27%, although its advantage over fixed few-shot prompting was uncertain (95% CI: -0.92 to 2.40 percentage points). One-shot prompting achieved the highest relation F1 of 6.95%, identifying directed relation extraction as the principal SmolLM2 bottleneck. Compared with fixed few-shot prompting, retrieval improved verbatim grounding (59.45% vs. 54.02%) but reduced complete structural compliance (33.3% vs. 42.7%). Verbatim matching establishes source presence rather than evidential relevance. An exploratory comparison using 35 benchmark narratives showed that Qwen3-8B achieved higher concept micro-F1 across all prompting conditions and higher relation F1 under demonstration-based prompting, reaching 51.37% and 34.62%, respectively, under one-shot prompting. The small subset limits generalization. These findings support evaluating semantic correctness, source traceability, structural reliability, and directed relation accuracy separately.

items.summary: This study evaluates the 1.7B SmolLM2-Instruct model on extracting safety knowledge from NTSB aviation accident narratives across concept accuracy, evidence grounding, structural compliance, and relation extraction, comparing zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting on 300 narratives. Evaluation combines structural checks, verbatim evidence matching, expert-reviewed semantic matching, and bootstrap confidence intervals. No single prompting strategy performed best across all dimensions, a useful cautionary result for small-model deployment in safety-critical text mining.

items.title: Multi-Party Authorization of Maintenance Prescriptions on a Permissioned Blockchain
items.content: arXiv:2611.34662v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, an equipment supplier's model may recommend an intervention that a plant schedules, a contractor executes, and a quality or safety function approves. A shared ledger records who submitted the prescription, yet cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule produced it. We require permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that calculation before releasing a work order. On a four-organization Hyperledger Fabric testbed using a public engine benchmark, this stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, whereas hash checks accepted four that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.

items.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
items.content: arXiv:2611.34868v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.

items.summary: This survey covers LLM risks and safeguards in telecommunications, introducing a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics to use cases such as customer service, network analytics, and operational support. It highlights open challenges including longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
items.reasoning: A useful domain-specific survey consolidating known LLM risk categories for telecom, but it is an aggregation of existing knowledge rather than original research and the domain framing limits general relevance.

items.title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
items.content: arXiv:2611.33652v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.
items.author: Zongshen Mu
items.summary: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework for portfolio management that incorporates tick-level intraday market dynamics such as order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations, with a risk-aware, clipped objective intended to stabilize learning in non-stationary markets. It combines self-supervised components with the RL loop to improve training stability.
items.reasoning: The topic is practically relevant but the contribution appears incremental, combining known RL stabilization techniques with domain-specific features. Single-author provenance, unclear baselines, and the difficulty of validating trading strategies out-of-sample limit confidence in broad impact.

items.title: Investigating the efficacy of vortex beam speckle patterns for the recognition of atmospheric turbulence and fractional topological charge with a deep learning model
items.content: arXiv:2611.34573v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fractional topological charge (TC) enlarges the usable mode set of orbital angular momentum (OAM) links, but reading it reliably after atmospheric turbulence remains difficult. Interferometric and diffractive methods need an undistorted beam and a careful alignment, while most learned approaches treat integer or coarsely spaced charges and do not include turbulence. Here we ask whether the charge of a scalar vortex beam can be regressed directly from a single speckle image, and at which turbulence strength this stops working. We propagate vortex beams over 1500~m through 150 von K\'arm\'an phase screens, scatter them with a fixed random diffuser, and record $256\times256$, 16-bit speckle images for TC from 0 to 10 in steps of 0.01 and turbulence strengths $D/r_0$ from 0 to 50; the results reported here use a subset of 20\,000 images, and a data set of $10^{6}$ images is in preparation. A convolutional neural network estimates the TC and, through an auxiliary head, the turbulence category. On charges withheld from training, the mean absolute error is 0.031 without turbulence (with a common intensity scale) and rises to 0.78 at $D/r_0=10$ and 1.85 at $D/r_0=50$, against 2.5 for a constant prediction, and the turbulence category is identified correctly in 78\% of the images. The results show that, at the present training size, the charge is read accurately only without turbulence, and that the charge and the turbulence oth act on the speckle grain size, which may limit the readout. Experimental validation and the extension to vector vortex beams are left for future work.

The work extends learned optical measurement approaches to regimes (fractional charge plus turbulence) where interferometric methods fail.

items.title: Feasibility-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-CU and O-DU Mapping in 6G O-RAN
items.content: arXiv:2611.34516v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper studies the mapping of the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the O-RAN central unit (O-CU) and O-RAN distributed unit (O-DU) onto virtual machines (VMs) in sixth-generation (6G) open radio access networks (O-RAN). The problem is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes the number of placed VNFCs and, secondarily, favors fewer active VMs and lower residual resource wastage. Although conventional optimization techniques can solve this problem, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for larger instances or when optimization must be repeated. To address this limitation, we explore two neural reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods: a deep $Q$-network (DQN) and a double deep $Q$-network (Double DQN). Whereas DQN uses the same target network to both select and evaluate the bootstrap action, Double DQN decouples these two operations to mitigate maximization-induced overestimation. We compare both methods against six baselines: random feasible placement, first-fit, first-fit decreasing, best-fit, a resource-wastage-aware heuristic, and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We conduct a controlled experimental evaluation across four problem sizes with $30$ independent instances each, together with capacity-stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation experiments. For the $16 \times 8$ VNFC-to-VM scenario, DQN and Double DQN achieve mean placed-VNFC fractions of $0.990$ and $0.996$, respectively. However, first-fit decreasing and the resource-wastage-aware heuristic match this placement quality with lower efficiency cost and lower decision time, whereas the MILP attains the lowest efficiency cost at a much higher runtime. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of neural placement for this static problem, without establishing superiority over conventional methods.

items.summary: The paper formulates mapping of O-RAN virtual network function components onto virtual machines in 6G networks as a feasibility-aware sequential decision problem maximizing placed components while minimizing active VMs and resource waste. Two deep RL methods (DQN and double DQN) are explored to avoid prohibitive repeated optimization costs for larger instances. It targets a concrete telecom deployment problem where learned policies must respect hard feasibility constraints.

items.title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.34649v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.

items.title: Why the Central Argument for Panpsychism Fails
items.content:
This is a crosspost from my Substack.

Fishing for the properties of consciousness

While many of my readers are philosophers, or have at least studied philosophy for a while at university, many are not. So I was reluctant to get into metaphysical debates within philosophy, fearing that they might get too high-brow, instead focusing on meta-philosophy which I believe is fairly easy to communicate.

But my discussions here with non-naturalist skeptics about consciousness science, such as with Philip Goff or Nino Kadic, inevitable get down to metaphysical arguments about intrinsic or categorical properties. Perhaps not surprising given that they are engaged in analytic metaphysics - a sub-discipline of philosophy that I’ve argued in a series of essays is a counter-Englightenment project not at all conducive to the central philosophical goal of understanding the world:

But while I may be able to show that their philosophical method is entirely misguided, panpsychists are not entirely unjustified by asking for a response to their central argument, even if the way by which they’ve arrived at should make us question whether it’s a good argument to begin with.

So due to repeated demand let me respond to one of the only two main arguments for panpsychism listed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article on panpsychism.

The so-called:

### The Intrinsic Nature Argument

(The other argument is the alleged inability for science to fully reduce conscious states to brain processes, which, as I’ve argued in yesterday’s post, reflects a mistaken radical reductionism among panpsychists that isn’t met by any other special science or for that matter folk ontology either. But as we’ll see this problem will come up again shortly.)

I’ve tried to make sure that it’s accessible to anyone without any knowledge of analytic metaphysics....

items.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
items.content: arXiv:2611.34025v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture.   By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.
items.author: Tjeng Wawan Cenggoro
items.summary: The paper proposes combining knowledge distillation with transfer learning so smaller EfficientNet variants can benefit from larger sibling models when adapting to new computer-vision tasks. The approach targets the common practice of using ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet backbones. It aims to improve downstream accuracy for compact models under limited data.
items.reasoning: Reasonable but incremental application of well-established distillation techniques to EfficientNet transfer learning. EfficientNet is an older architecture by current standards, and the contribution offers limited novelty or broad impact.

items.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.33175v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

items.summary: The study evaluates a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach for DeBERTa-based automated writing scoring of middle-school ELA responses, establishing explanatory fidelity before interpreting feature importance across 61 linguistic features. items.title: Robust Adaptive Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted mmWave Massive MIMO via a Stochastic Shannon Entropy Criterion
items.content: arXiv:2611.33773v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems remains challenging due to the passive nature of the RIS, the high dimensionality of the cascaded channel, and the presence of non-Gaussian impulsive disturbances. This paper proposes a robust sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, termed reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy (RZA-SSE), for angular-domain channel estimation. The algorithm combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized \(\ell_1\) penalty. Both the data-driven term and the nonsmooth penalty are differentiated using exact Wirtinger calculus. An exact weight-error recursion and a mean-square energy relation are derived. Local stability is analyzed via a joint coefficient--penalty state representation, and an approximate steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD) expression is obtained. Extensive simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise demonstrate that ZA-SSE consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD.

items.title: Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Brain Tumour Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.34781v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate and early classification of brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for treatment planning, yet many published deep learning studies are trained and tested on small, single-source datasets, reporting accuracies that may not hold outside these datasets. This study compares six deep learning architectures for four-class classification (healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour): a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), an attention-based CNN, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50 and Xception augmented with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The models were trained on a corpus assembled from four publicly available MRI datasets. Because these datasets carry no patient identifiers, a leakage-aware pipeline was developed that removes exact duplicates using MD5 hashing (550 images) and near-duplicates using perceptual hashing (8,024 images), and assigns visually similar images to the same fold during 5-fold group cross-validation. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test on a fully held-out dataset was used to measure cross-dataset generalisation. Under a conventional random split, ShuffleNet achieved 97.1% accuracy with 1.2M parameters. Under leakage-aware group K-fold cross-validation, ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) were statistically indistinguishable (paired t-test, p = 0.19), and both significantly outperformed the custom CNNs. On the held-out dataset, accuracy dropped for every model: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best (78.4%), while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%. Glioma-meningioma confusion was the dominant error mode, and Grad-CAM maps showed that predictions were driven by tumour regions. These results indicate that in-distribution accuracy alone overstates real-world performance and that leakage-aware and cross-dataset evaluation should be reported alongside it.
items.author: Prisha Gupta, Pradeep Kumar Gupta
items.summary: The study compares six deep learning architectures, including a baseline CNN, attention CNN, ShuffleNet, and CBAM-augmented EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50, and Xception, for four-class brain tumour classification from MRI. It addresses a known weakness of prior work by training on a corpus assembled from four public MRI datasets rather than a single small source. This improves the external validity of architecture comparisons in a clinically relevant task.
items.reasoning: A competent comparative study with better dataset practices than much of the MRI classification literature, but it applies established architectures without novel methods, and clinical validation or prospective data remains absent.

items.title: "A Republic of LessWrong Letters"—A Letter to DirectedEvolution
items.content:
My dearest @DirectedEvolution,

We've both been thinking about how to strengthen the writing culture on LessWrong. I think we agree that LessWrong has many great writers (more, I'd say) when compared to the past, and yet still feel that something has been lost.

You raise an excellent hypothesis in your recent essay No Comment. It's not that the writers are less intellectually sophisticated, or their ideas less good, or their writing less fun (though they should be having more fun!). The primary change is that we're talking with each other less than we used to.

You point out that LessWrong authors comment less than they used to, and while I'd add that the absolute amount of writing is up, we can be absolutely sure of your claim on a relative level. Recall this chart from Lightcone's 2024 fundraiser.

(I have updated it to include the last two years of data.)

Again, absolute wordcount is up. However, after we realize that the light blue corresponds to posts and the dark blue to comments, we can see that LessWrong 1.0 was characterized by a roughly 10-to-1 ratio of comments to posts, and LessWrong 2.0 is about a 1-to-1 ratio of comments to posts. This is a drastic change in site culture.

Historical aside. You probably know this, but in case not (and also because I like getting the chance to talk about it), the change is largely due to the algorithm for showing posts on the frontpage.

On LessWrong 2.0, we have an algorithm for showing posts that is directly proportional to recency and karma. On LessWrong 1.0 there was no algorithm, it just showed whatever the latest post was that had been posted. Even if it was utter trash, everyone on LessWrong was looking at it together, the eye of Sauron turning its gaze to you, and this was the topic that everyone was speaking about. The comments were intense and multitudinous....

items.summary: Ben Pace responds to an essay on declining comment culture on LessWrong, presenting updated data showing the comment-to-post wordcount ratio fell from roughly 10-to-1 on LessWrong 1.0 to about 1-to-1 on 2.0. The letter explores how to strengthen the site's writing and dialogue culture, proposing a letters-style exchange.

items.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
items.content: arXiv:2611.33432v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.

items.title: Spectral Colorimetry Based on GMoE for Temperature Measurement in Explosion Fields
items.content: arXiv:2611.33750v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spectroscopic thermometry in explosion fields has attracted considerable attention in related engineering domains, primarily because it can mitigate the interference of traditional contact methods with temperature distributions and address the limitations of high-temperature measurement scenarios. However, existing physics-model-driven methods typically rely on regressing a single radiance-ratio pair, which limits their adaptability to wide-range temperature estimation. This limitation arises from notable variations in the mapping between grayscale ratios and radiance ratios at different temperatures. In contrast, existing data-driven methods often suffer from limited performance due to the scarcity of training data, a challenge exacerbated by the sensitivity of explosion fields. In this work, we propose a gated mixture of experts (GMoE) framework that integrates a divide-and-conquer strategy in deep learning with physical prior knowledge for temperature estimation, thereby decomposing the complex task into multiple expert-specific subtasks. Specifically, each expert is developed using physically calibrated polynomial functions to model the relationship between grayscale ratios and radiance ratios for a given pair of spectral bands, with temperature then estimated using a physical model incorporating the corresponding parameters. Additionally, a gating network is designed to adaptively weight the outputs of different experts and generate the final temperature estimate. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the best performance when implemented with the Transformer-based gating network, yielding a mean RMSE of $12.70 \pm 1.32$ K and a mean MAE of $7.96 \pm 0.86$ K. Compared with conventional spectral colorimetry, the proposed framework reduces the mean RMSE and MAE by 63.4\% and 70.8\%, respectively.
items.author: Jie Fang, Wenhao Li, Jianning Yang, Nan Wang
items.summary: This work applies a Gaussian mixture-of-experts (GMoE) approach to spectroscopic thermometry in explosion fields, addressing the narrow adaptability of physics-model-driven radiance-ratio regression and the data scarcity problem of data-driven methods. It aims to widen the range of accurate high-temperature estimation without contact interference. It is a specialized engineering application of mixture models to a physics measurement problem.
items.reasoning: Niche domain application with limited relevance to mainstream AI research directions; the methodological novelty (GMoE for radiance ratio mapping) appears modest. Useful for the defense/explosives engineering community but low broader impact.

items.title: A Therapist's Guide to the Singularity
items.content:
I'm a therapist who has been following AI alignment for the last few years. In that time, I've been dumbfounded by two things. First, how fast capabilities have progressed throughout this year. We expected things to move fast and they still managed to exceed our expectations. Second, how few people grasp the gravity of the situation, particularly within my own field.

Mental health clinicians are tasked with helping people navigate society's blind spots, so we need to understand what is coming. Yet it is rare to find another clinician who truly understands the real implications of AI. Most of them dismiss it as a hype bubble, or as an exaggeration the labs use to get regulatory capture, largely because they don't see what makes AI different from past technological shifts.

I want this post to be a first resource for the stress and anxiety currently plaguing AI researchers, with the hope of developing more resources in the future. I'm also working on training licensed therapists to bring them up to speed, and I'll have a question for you about that at the end.

## What's happening to AI researchers

From the studies I've read[1]and the AI researchers I've talked to, many in the field are operating on high alert. That state can be useful in short bursts, but the problem is that researchers have been stuck in this hypervigilant state for years. They check the news and Twitter anxiously. They use guilt and anxiety as fuel to keep pushing harder. A lot of researchers work in brutally fast sprints that deplete their energy and result in burnout. They feel ashamed of their own human limitations, and that shame drives them right back to another sprint....

items.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
items.content: arXiv:2611.33322v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

items.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.33163v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.

It addresses the challenge of detecting skilled forgeries from static raster images.

items.title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets
items.content: arXiv:2611.34779v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In a Houston 2024 replay, replacing a fixed 20 percent battery reserve with a county-risk threshold raises observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0 percent to 86.5 percent and adds USD 10.2 in modeled annualized margin per home (paired 95 percent interval: USD +1.7 to USD +21.7). The paired coverage-gain interval includes zero. This is a conditional simulation result, not measured company reliability. Residential batteries face this tradeoff because market discharge consumes energy also needed for household outages. We release HomeFleet-ERCOT, combining observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs. We compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs; ten promise-cost candidates span 31.1 percent-96.3 percent backup coverage. Of these, 10 have lower modeled margin than fixed 20 percent, and 3 also have lower coverage. Chronological, geographic, fleet, and storm tests examine transfer. An alert charging override has a conditional energy-and-power sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5 percent of 41 county mass-outage episodes provide enough continuous warning for every battery preset. Synthetic tests include short, missed, and false warnings, load uplift, capacity loss, and dropout. A static AC audit retains existing feeder violations; aging comparisons expose model sensitivity. The released benchmark, controllers, and checkpoints provide a reproducible basis for comparing these tradeoffs. This work supports the design of residential battery programs that assess market value and household backup service together.

The authors honestly note the coverage-gain interval includes zero, that results are conditional simulations, and they release the HomeFleet-ERCOT dataset with causal controller inputs.

items.content:
Now that I can delegate problems to AI, I've been going back over some
of my old projects to do them better and more in depth.
Friday this
was my

rent
map, earlier it was my

mixer,

rhythm stage
setup,

bass
whistle, and

clipboard
normalizer.  Today I'm picking back up my

Boston
transit quality map:

(interactive version)

In 2010 I made a map,
which I'd wanted for a while,
showing how well you can get around on transit.  Each point
represented the average travel time to every other point.  Iterating
on it with Claude, this version improves it in a bunch of ways:

- Originally I built this by post-processing a set of maps Dan Tillberg made; now it
routes directly from MBTA GTFS data.

- OpenStreetMap for walking times, instead of (guessing; I don't
have Tillberg's source code) straight-line distance.

- For simplicity, the original map treated every destination as
equally valuable.  Aside from being unrealistic, this also unfairly
advantaged the center of the map.  The new one can weight by jobs or
residents (both from the Census).

- It no longer estimates over water or other inaccessible areas.

- It builds maps annually going back to 2009, and lets you
explore the ways areas have gotten better or worse transit over
time. ( interactive history page)

Overall, things have gotten substantially slower.  Here's 2009 vs
2026, with areas that got slower in orange, and the areas that got
faster are in purple:

Let's start with the four bright spots.  The biggest improvement is
Assembly Square, which got an infill station
on the Orange Line in 2014.  Here's the year-over-year comparison,
showing a ~6min improvement in an area that now has 1.6k residents and
10k jobs:

The other three spots are good, but a smaller impact:

- Chelsea gained the SL3, which
improved service north of the Chelsea St Bridge.  This covers ~500
residents and ~1.1k jobs....

items.title: On Utilization of Edge-AI for condition monitoring towards predictive maintenance: A use case in dairy processing using explainable AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.34563v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are driving Industry 4.0, enhancing productivity, automation, and efficiency in manufacturing systems. This study develops an Edge-AI-based condition monitoring framework, as a step towards predictive maintenance, for a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant, using vibration data collected via a low-power IIoT sensor node and processed on an edge device.
items.author: Rahul Umesh Mhapsekar, Norah O'Shea, Omer Ali, Steven Davy, Lizy Abraham
items.summary: This paper presents an edge-AI condition monitoring framework for a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant, using vibration data from a low-power IIoT sensor node processed on an edge device, with explainable AI, as a step toward predictive maintenance. It is an applied Industry 4.0 case study rather than a methodological advance. Its value lies in demonstrating feasibility of low-power edge deployment with interpretability in a real industrial setting.

items.title: Nepali Currency Denomination Classification Using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and MobileNetV2: An Experimental Comparison
items.content: arXiv:2611.33713v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automated currency denomination recognition is a computer vision task with applications in cash handling, financial technology, and assistive systems. This study classifies seven Nepali currency denominations (Rs. 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, and 1,000) using three configurations: a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN), MobileNetV2 with transfer learning, and MobileNetV2 with hyperparameter tuning. A compiled dataset of 16,249 images was used, comprising 10,500 training, 3,500 validation, and 2,249 independent test images. Images were resized to 128 x 128 pixels, normalized, and augmented to vary orientation, scale, illumination, and appearance. Models were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and precision-recall and ROC analysis. The hyperparameter-tuned MobileNetV2 achieved the highest validation accuracy (95\%), with precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.93, 0.91, and 0.92, but reached only 84\% accuracy on the held-out test set. MobileNetV2 with transfer learning but no additional tuning achieved 89\% test accuracy, and the conventional CNN achieved 85\%. Transfer learning therefore provided a competitive approach under the evaluated conditions, while higher validation accuracy from tuning did not yield higher test accuracy. To demonstrate practical deployment, a Flask-based web prototype using TensorFlow Lite was developed, supporting image upload and live webcam recognition with both visual and voice output. The study shows the feasibility of combining lightweight deep learning with a voice-assisted web interface for Nepali currency recognition, and highlights the need for more diverse datasets, greater robustness under uncontrolled imaging conditions, and broader real-world evaluation.
