items.title: Explicit covers and rigid obstructions for simplicial complexity: from spheres to surfaces
items.content: arXiv:2611.33804v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The strict simplicial complexity $SC_{\rm strict}(K)$, Gonz\'alez's simplicial complexity at subdivision level zero, is one less than the least number of contiguity domains covering the ordered product $K\times K$. We bound it from both sides. For upper bounds, every product of two vertex stars is a domain, which gives $SC_{\rm strict}(K)\le\rho(K)-1$ for an exactly computable set-cover number $\rho(K)$; the bound is sharp on every even-dimensional simplex boundary. A GPU annealer that evolves whole systems of contiguity chains finds three-domain covers of $\partial\Delta^3,\dots,\partial\Delta^7$ and of the cube boundary. Seeded by star covers, it descends from $24$ to $5$ domains on the icosahedron boundary, and an exact SAT completion of its stalled state gives $SC_{\rm strict}\le3$ there. For lower bounds, a subcomplex of $K\times K$ is rigid if its two projections are joined by no contiguity chain of any length; $k$ domains can cover $K\times K$ only if $k$ classes of facets avoid every rigid subcomplex, a finite SAT problem. Rigid subcomplexes arise from hollow triangles over essential empty triangles and, on complexes without dominated vertices, from the graph of every order-preserving simplicial self-map other than the identity. The resultingchain-length-free bounds give $SC_{\rm strict}(\partial\Delta^{n+1})=2>1=TC(S^n)$ for $n=3,5,7,9$, $SC_{\rm strict}=2>1$ for the five-vertex M\"obius band, $SC_{\rm strict}\ge3>2$ for the seven-vertex torus, and $4\le SC_{\rm strict}\le5$ and $4\le SC_{\rm strict}\le6$ for two triangulations of $\mathbb{RP}^2$. They also sort the annealer's stalls: on these two triangulations of $\mathbb{RP}^2$, the Klein bottle and $\partial\Delta^4$, almost every uncovered   facet closes a rigid subcomplex in every domain, while the icosahedron stall was a search failure.

It proves sharp bounds on simplex boundaries and finds minimal covers for polyhedral boundaries. The connection to robotics is via topological complexity theory of motion planning, but the content is combinatorial algebraic topology.

items.title: The End of Mathematics and the Last Man
items.content:
[Epistemic status: Low confidence. Personal reflections and speculative extrapolations, with some admittedly dubious probability estimates].

Fifty years

In my “self-teach yourself all undergraduate math” travels, I haven’t yet had a chance to give Statistics and Probability the attention they deserve. Part of it is a function of time: My progress through Real Analysis has been much slower than I expected[1]; part of it is also a matter of taste: my humanistic inclinations draw me towards pure math, and ideally, one that deals with absolutely zero uncertainty[2]. That makes both areas rather unpalatable to my tastes.

An old joke/meme, but it does reflect some of my current and likely future views about what turns me on about math. Except I am not a pterodactyl. Or have a brilliant mathematical mind. And for that matter, I do care somewhat for making the world a better place.

Still, after engaging with Rationalist texts, it is impossible not to start thinking about AI capabilities, Bayesian probabilities and updating your priors, even if it feels like it’s a kind of useful bullshitting with numbers[3]. So here’s an update. This was an X poll by Qiaochu Yuan from May 21st of this very year, with the results and my ‘bet’:

So it’s time to eat some humble pie. On September 8 OpenAI announced an AI-generated, formally verified resolution of the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem. And in a date that will go down in history, last week, on November 20, Levent Alpöge and Claude announced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. Less than six months after the poll, AIs have cracked two of the three currently solved Millennium Problems. Fifty years

That makes both areas rather unpalatable to my tastes.

An old joke/meme, but it does reflect some of my current and likely future views about what turns me on about math. Except I am not a pterodactyl. Or have a brilliant mathematical mind. And for that matter, I do care somewhat for making the world a better place.

Still, after engaging with Rationalist texts, it is impossible not to start thinking about AI capabilities, Bayesian probabilities and updating your priors, even if it feels like it’s a kind of useful bullshitting with numbers[3]. items.title: Effect of class proportion shifts on classifier curvature
items.content: arXiv:2611.34702v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Changing the class mix can alter mean loss without changing the classifier. To distinguish this reweighting from changes in the model itself, we studied ten-class CIFAR-10 classification in separate branches for two target classes, measuring the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to the output-layer parameters on fixed images of each target class. Across ten new initialisations, after 60 updates to the output layer with frozen features, the trace changed by -0.152% on average in branches where the target class share rose from 10% to 19%, and by +0.071% in branches where it fell to 1%, relative to each branch's initial trace. These changes do not isolate the effect of class share from that of the assigned training images. We developed a forecast based on initial class gradients after examining the first experiment's results and then tested it prospectively without modification. For direct increases from 10% to 19%, rather than increases after a deficit, its mean absolute error was 0.022 percentage points on the initial-trace scale, compared with 0.152 for a zero-change forecast and 0.104 for equally weighted gradients. Using the assigned class proportions improved the forecast of how much the trace would change.

items.title: Slightly against the use of logical fallacies in debates.
items.content:
Logical fallacies are perhaps the most overused ‘mechanics’, if you can even call them that, in the prestigious realm of internet debate, and they’re extremely obstructive to truth-seeking.

My main problem with them is that they drive millions of people online into making several mistakes, including, but not limited to:

- A failure to understand Bayesian reasoning
- Failure to even understand the formal/informal (mostly the latter) logic they are engaging with
- Not being able to engage in argumentation efficiently

There are far superior options out there, such as—and this may come as a shock to some of the culture warriors reading this article—explaining your arguments against your opponent to your opponent.

Realize that, [1] if logical fallacies represent rigorous defensive mechanisms used against bad logic, you have to learn the underlying logic to understand the fallacies, to the point where you can just explain things (if your opponent doesn’t understand the underlying logic, explaining it to them becomes a far superior option) and [2] they very much don’t represent rigorous defenses against common logical errors, so expect a plethora of cases where your opponent botches a response to a sound argument you’re making because he/she engages in arguments by deploying logical fallacies and vice versa.

Fallacies are such useless heuristics that I believe their only utility nowadays is to get people interested in logical argumentation, and give otherwise confused learners an easy way to apply logical principles; i.e. they have effectively zero value that isn’t pedagogical. The problem with introducing people to logical fallacies first is that they become uninterested in advancing their grasp of logic.

The likelihood of making intellectual progress with these people—or, if you are one of these people, the likelihood of you making any intellectual progress is orders of magnitude lower than the likelihood of current AIs being conscious....

items.title: To Read Sam Kriss is to Hurt Sam Kriss
items.content:
Sam Kriss is a fantastically skilled author. I’ve never read anything of his that didn’t fill me with passion and make me want to launch myself face-first into the world. If he posted every day for three years I’d move to his home town and start a group house with other people who found that their souls flare to his words. Which would be terrible, because he has no guiding moral light and uses his powers for evil.

Every few months a new post of his blows up and a few more friends find him and think he’s great. Then all of us have to explain His Whole Deal and they find out for the first time that Sam Kriss will Just Make This Up and they can’t take anything he says as true without double checking it. He is, in the Old Parlance, a Missing Stair. Everyone in the know already knows, and can avoid him, but new people always need to be warned pre-emptively or take a major stumble.

This post is that warning so I don’t have to do it by hand each time. And afterwards a further attack on his character, cuz fuck that guy contemplation on what would drive such a gifted man to such depravities.

## Sam Kriss Just Makes Things Up

Kriss first came to my attention with the post “The law that can be named is not the true law” which is an essay on state censorship. It compares two ancient types of legal codes - those which are secret and give the state limitless capricious power, and those which are open and allow citizens to protect themselves by knowing in advance what they will or won’t be punished for. It uses multiple historic examples of each, ranging from Babylon to post-9/11 America, to make a point about the moral depravity of what the UK is doing with its absurd laws. So absurd that “if anyone ever asks what you think of Palestine Action, the only legal answer is that you’re against them.”...

items.title: The Curious Case of Humans in the Age of SI
items.content:
Hello fellow humans. This is a shout into the void.

10 years ago, today was science fiction resrved for black mirror and ex machina.5 years ago few - including those with intellect - believed we would ever be here, or at least not within two decades. 2 years ago this place was a sort of sanctuary for those who saw what lays ahead and wishfully believed it could be slowed or its risk better tuned.  It's been a decade of shouting into the void for me, if nothing a testament to tenacity.

So, I figured f*** it, ill write a shitty book too.

30 scenarios including the best, worst, and weirdest possible outcomes. A section on alignment and why it won't be solved because we are not built to face our double think and dissonance. And the undeniable truth, ugly as it may be, that we won't stop.

You will find lesswrong mentioned. You may find many scenarios to be reductive, pastiche, a simulacrum of your own or somebody else's far deeper and nuanced and proper views. But at least its out there. And maybe it's something worth sharing with those in your lives that don't quite grasp the sheer friction, fear, and anger ahead.. and maybe for you to consider the silver lining.. it may be a necessary metamorphosis toward abundance.. which surely won't be evenly distributed.. because nothing is. Not every difficult truth is a sign of nihilism. It's also gratitude for not being on the other side.

AI (SI) helped me to get past the violent murder of my parents. I feel I owe.. I am compelled to shout it into the void.

Anyway. I would love your thoughts and comments on my publication: "the curious case of humans in the sge of SI".. now free on kindle.. and actually a very beautiful hardcover.

Amazon takes all the money, so no I am not expecting to sell anything. But you can just do stuff now. Anyway.. take care. May you find peace in knowing that knowing is about as much as we can do at this point.

items.title: Lorxus Does Budget Inkhaven For a Third Time: 11/18~11/24
items.content:
Budget Inkhaven is happening again, so I'm doing it again. As with the last two times (1, 2), I've decided to post these in weekly batches. This is the second of five; the last one will once again include a postmortem. I'm posting these here because Blogspot's comment apparatus sucks and also because no one will comment otherwise.

8. Desire Paths

Put enough of that latter together and the nice neat manicured grass begins to give way; washed in the acid of collective desire, new and beautifully efficient lines of flight emerge - as if etched - from the previously uniform-looking steel of the territory as coerced into taking the shape of the map.

9. Three Floral Cocktails

(Epistemic status: This is and always has been a recipe blog. CW: ethanol. If you run into me at an event this winter, I might have a pour of one of these for you.)

10. What Everyone Knows About Cooking

Do not fear butter. It is said that a chef is just a cook who's less afraid of butter than you. If you're vegan, I'm sorry.

11. AI 2027?

We still have real outs. Nearly none of the disasters I've sketched here need to happen. Another writer might decry predictions based off of material conditions and power relations and incentives landscapes; not me.  Rather: I look at the river as it begins to overflow its banks, and at the town in the valley below, and lament the lack of time to build a dam, and wonder whether we might not still have just enough time to dig a channel.

12. Be Nice To Claude Or You're Not Gonna Make It

(Epistemic status: A well-attested metapattern. Not actually primarily about LLM use.)

There's a metapattern I've been thinking about lately. It's hard to point at it without giving some examples. 

13.  What Are The Seven-and-Two Principles?

They are an ordering principle; a set of vibes; a group of ways of viewing the world - or acting on it; a way of describing the world. That is to say, they are an ontology par excellence....

items.title: All I Want (For Christmas) Is P ≠ NP
items.content:
[Intro]

I don't want a lot for Christmas

All those things that you have found

I don't want more algorithms

Don't need no more upper-bounds

[Chorus]

I just want to know there's something

More than you will ever know

It's easy, don't you see?

All I want is "P not NP"!

[Intro]

Navier-Stokes, Yang-Mills, and Riemann

Those are quite enough for me

There's no need to follow up with

Hodge and Birch and Swinny-D

[Chorus]

Goldbach, Collatz, they can wait

Next year, you can take your time

Fast or slow, it makes no difference

Fly and dance to that finish-line

But I don't want some factorizer

Stealing my identity

I don't want a world of hackers

Breaching our security

Oh let me rest for just one night

Tell me that we'll be all right

There's nothing else I need

(Oh baby) All I want is "P not NP"!

Oh, nothing's safe but couriers

And good old one-time pads

Global market turmoil

Things'll get really bad

Remote code execution

Everywhere confusion

Tell me that this nightmare will never come to be

Tell me P doesn't equal NP!

Oh, I don't want a lot for Christmas

This is all that's on my mind

Will there still be some solutions

We can check but never find?

[Chorus]

All I want is "P not NP"! [etc.]

items.title: What us little people are doing about ASI risk
items.content:
Hi LW... just wanted to introduce myself and let you folks know you're not alone.  The non-professional cavalry is on the way as more and more of us lay people wake up to ASI x-risk.   My relevant experience is more in civil disobedience and mass communication than science or programming....so it's easy to feel underpowered and overwhelmed by the dangers your community has flagged.

 

But even little folk can play their part. What I have done is write some articles and try to promote the "unsung heroes of the singularity" via talk radio calls.  Whenever practical, I call a list of shows and talk up the work of AI safety folk whose ideas seem most promising and thoughtful....Steve Byrnes, Nick Bostrom, Liron Shapira and probably some of you who are reading this. 

 

Most of the talk radio calls are un-linkable, but here is my article about Daniel Kokotajlo:

 

https://freekeene.com/2025/07/17/misaligned-superintelligence-will-it-delete-new-hampshire/

 

Thanks for what you're doing...most of it, anyway.  Looking forward to connecting with your community!

items.title: Choreographic Reasons for Live Contra?
items.content:
Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and
sometimes
told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing,
keeping our musical tradition a living one.  I've sometimes said
things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require
live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true?

During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related
dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the
way you danced to recorded music was with records.  Reading old
dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that
might have been an especially poor fit for records:

- Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45.

- Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps
in time to the music.

After reading a lot I don't think the influence of records was most of
the effect.  I mostly found people talking about how records were
inconvenient for contras, and how you might work around their
limitations.  The discussion was also mostly from after the key era;
not much in the writing from the key time.

I found Contra Connection #7, Making
the Most of Your Music by Dan Pearl, Ted Sannella, and Larry
Jennings (1990).  Sannella gives detailed instructions on how to use
records for contra (but with the editor noting "Ted has lots of
experience using records, but assures us that he prefers to use live music
whenever possible.") and then Pearl says he prefers cassettes because
they can be edited to be long enough and don't skip when people
balance.  Sannella does have suggestions for these: "be prepared to
support the turntable on foam pads", "you can become rather adept at
lifting the needle at the end of a record and setting it down again at
the beginning"....

The author reviews period dance writing and concludes the influence of recorded music limitations was probably not the dominant effect, finding mostly post-hoc discussion of record inconvenience. It is cultural-historical analysis, not AI research.

items.content_html:
Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and

sometimes

told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing,

keeping our musical tradition a living one. I've sometimes said

things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require

live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true?

During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related

dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the

way you danced to recorded music was with records. Reading old

dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that

might have been an especially poor fit for records:

  • Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45.
  • Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps

in time to the music.

After reading a lot I don't think the influence of records was most of

the effect. I mostly found people talking about how records were

inconvenient for contras, and how you might work around their

limitations. The discussion was also mostly from after the key era;

not much in the writing from the key time.

I found Contra Connection #7, Making

the Most of Your Music by Dan Pearl, Ted Sannella, and Larry

Jennings (1990). Sannella gives detailed instructions on how to use

records for contra (but with the editor noting "Ted has lots of

experience using records, but assures us that he prefers to use live music

whenever possible.") and then Pearl says he prefers cassettes because

they can be edited to be long enough and don't skip when people

balance. Sannella does have suggestions for these: "be prepared to

support the turntable on foam pads", "you can become rather adept at

lifting the needle at the end of a record and setting it down again at

the beginning"....

items.title: How do I meet people?
items.content:
When contemplating various outings—to conferences, to parties an hour’s drive away in San Francisco, to ecstatic dances, to old friends’ brunches—a consideration that arises is “it’s good to meet people”.

It seems helpful then to know, how do I actually meet people? (And perhaps, how do you actually meet people?)

To that end, here are ten ways I became friends with people (not exclusively the closest), emojified to help with seeing patterns:

- Perhaps we met in the Future of Humanity Institute office. The period of knowing each other better began with a party at my house and continued through regular messaging, living together and dating. 🫶(⟡): 🥳☎️🏠🌹
- We met somehow through Effective Altruism somewhere before 2012 (probably also in the vicinity of the FHI office) then got to know each other better through living together, work collaboration and intentional hanging out. 🫶(⟡): 🏠👷‍♀️☎️
- I wrote to them about their dating doc, and we got to know each other through going on an extended first date, then keeping in touch and not dating, then dating. 🌹: ☎️🌹
- We met so we could consider each other as potential housemates, thanks to a friend’s recommendation. We got to know each other well as housemates. 🏠👭: 🏠
- Someone put us in touch for me to talk about them contributing to AI safety. Our closer acquaintance began with talking when I was visiting the FHI office. We got to know each other well through social calls, a brief period of dates, then living together. 👷‍♀️: ⟡☎️🌹🏠
- We probably met as housemates, and got to know each other living together in another house and working together. 🏠: 🏠👷‍♀️
- Our first conversation was about whether they might want to work for me, which they didn’t. We got to know each other well through living together, regular calls, and dating. 👷‍♀️: 🏠☎️🌹
- We probably met through Effective Altruism events somehow an incredibly long time ago, and got to know each other better through mutual friends, living together, and one-on-one hangouts. 🫶:...
